The marker is the harbour; the airfield raids of 1941–43 are under Castel Benito. A Zuckerman Archive catalogue entry (University of East Anglia) for a 1943 Allied report on the effects of air raids on Tripoli says the city was attacked 209 times from the air between 15 June 1940 and the Allied occupation on 23 January 1943; it gives no casualty or damage figures. An Australian War Memorial caption for a 26 January 1943 photograph says heavy bombers of the US and British air forces hit the port, that the harbour took the brunt and that few bombs fell in the residential quarter.

name: Ibn al-Sheikh al-Libi found dead in his cell at Abu Salim, May 2009
ar: العثور على ابن الشيخ الليبي ميتاً في زنزانته بأبو سليم، مايو 2009
relevance: A man returned from US custody died in a Tripoli prison; the authorities called it suicide and gave no access to the evidence.
text: Amnesty's 2010 report says Abdelaziz Al-Fakheri, also known as Ibn Al Sheikh Al Libi, who had been returned from US custody and held since, was reported to have died by suicide in Abu Salim on 9 May 2009; the authorities opened an investigation and later said he killed himself but gave no details. The US State Department's report for the same year says he was found dead in his cell from an apparent suicide, that Amnesty was denied access to his guards, forensic doctors and the autopsy report, and that no results of the Libyan investigation were public by the end of the year. The two reports spell his name differently. Nobody outside the prison has shown whether it was suicide. Human Rights Watch, in its report on renditions, says Libyan authorities called his death a suicide and that photographs it saw show bruising on parts of his body; the report does not name the prison.

name: Clashes between prisoners and guards at Abu Salim, 4 October 2006
ar: اشتباكات بين السجناء والحراس في أبو سليم، 4 أكتوبر 2006
relevance: One prisoner was reported killed and others injured in a disturbance ten years after the 1996 killings.
text: The US State Department's report for 2006 says, citing press accounts, that clashes between prisoners and guards at Abu Salim on 4 October 2006 killed one prisoner, Hafed Mansour Al-Zwai, and injured 17. The Abu Salim pin carries an earlier account of the same day that says security forces reportedly killed at least one prisoner and wounded at least nine, so the injury count differs between sources. The State Department gives no further details, and I found no independent report of the cause.

name: Shooting at a Tripoli football match, July 1996
ar: إطلاق نار في مباراة كرة قدم بطرابلس، يوليو 1996
relevance: Spectators were shot at after a crowd chanted against the government; the stadium is not named in the 1996 reports.
text: A compilation of the contemporary press reports says a match between the Tripoli rivals Al-Ittihad and Al-Ahli ended in a brawl and shooting, with spectators fleeing or stampeding. The Independent says supporters invaded the pitch after a controversial goal, chanting anti-government slogans; the Washington Post quotes diplomats saying bodyguards loyal to Gaddafi's sons fired at spectators and that some in the crowd shot back. Libyan state television put the toll at 8 killed and 39 injured on 14 July; unofficial estimates range from about 20 (an exile source in the Post) to up to 50 (The Independent). The date varies between reports (the Guardian says 9 July, AP points to Friday 12 July), and the 1996 reports do not name the stadium. Later sources say it was the June 11 Stadium, which that compilation could not verify, so the marker sits between the June 11 Stadium and the 7 October Stadium with a wide radius. The justice minister announced an investigation; I found no outcome.

name: Police raid on Ethiopian and Eritrean migrants in Gurji, September 2003
ar: مداهمة الشرطة لمهاجرين إثيوبيين وإريتريين في قرجي، سبتمبر 2003
relevance: More than 100 migrants, including women and children, were arrested and beaten in a residential district.
text: Human Rights Watch's 2006 report on migrants says police arrested more than 100 Ethiopians and Eritreans, including women and children, in the Gurgee suburb of Tripoli in September 2003, that the men were beaten with sticks and a plastic pipe, that detainees' savings were taken without a receipt, and that guards later called them “spies for Israel”. It places this in a wider August 2003 police campaign of broad sweeps that included raids on four migrant areas. The report does not give the street or the place where they were held, so the marker is the district.

name: Tripoli anti-Jewish riot, 12 June 1948
ar: أعمال الشغب ضد اليهود في طرابلس، يونيو 1948
relevance: A second wave of anti-Jewish violence in the old city, three years after the 1945 pogrom.
text: Wikipedia’s account, drawn from a British Public Information Office report, says the day was calm until about 16:10 on Saturday 12 June 1948, when a Jewish youth and an Arab argued at the junction of Via Leopardi and Corso Sicilia and a fight ran down Via Leopardi. A crowd of Arabs then moved towards the Jewish quarter of the old city by Bab el Horria, Via Manzoni and Via Leopardi, and by about 16:40 roughly 500 people, mostly boys, were throwing stones from waste ground west of Via Leopardi while looting began in nearby houses. Jews fought back from rooftops and the city walls with bombs and small arms; police fired after a bomb and gunfire came from the roofs, ordered a general stand-to at 17:40 and imposed a curfew from 19:00 to 06:00. The article says 13 or 14 Jews and four Muslims were killed and 38 Jews and 51 Muslims injured; other Wikipedia pages say 12 or 14 Jews, and Lyn Julius says 14. About 280 Jewish homes were destroyed and some 300 families left destitute. Sources disagree about blame: the British report pointed to visiting volunteers and ‘a certain aggressive spirit’ among Jewish youth, while the Chief Administrator said the outbreak was spontaneous with no sign of planning; the British also found signs of Jewish organisation and said the Jewish side’s role ‘was not purely defence’, and a US consul wrote in November 1948 that the Jewish community had become more aggressive. Jewish emigration rose afterwards: 30,972 Jews left for Israel between 1948 and 1951. The report names streets but the sources give no coordinates, so the marker is the old city with a 1 km radius.

name: Tripoli anti-Jewish riots, 5 June 1967
ar: أعمال العنف ضد اليهود في طرابلس، يونيو 1967
relevance: The last major riot against the Jewish community, after which almost all of it left for Italy.
text: Wikipedia says that on the night of 5 June 1967, the day the Six-Day War began, a mob of hundreds attacked Jewish homes and businesses in Tripoli’s Jewish Quarter, burned the Bet-El synagogue to the ground and set houses, shops and cars on fire; it says 60% of all Jewish assets were destroyed, 18 Jews were killed and at least 25 injured. King Idris’s secret police then moved about 3,000 Jews to a former British military base in the desert; during the move, rioters disguised as police are said to have kidnapped and killed nine members of the Luzon family, two parents and seven children. A witness who was eight at the time, Doris Nachum, told the JIMENA oral history project that the rioting lasted until about 11 pm, that her family hid in a neighbour’s attic in a house built over a synagogue, that more than 3,000 Jews were held at a base about 45 minutes from the capital, and that the seven Luzon sons were killed and their bodies burned in pigment kilns; her account is a single witness and reposted second-hand. Alitalia staff sheltered Jews at the airport, and about 4,100 reached Italy, 2,500 of them on Alitalia flights to Rome. US State Department files add that ‘angry demonstrations and attacks against U.S. offices in Libya’ followed the outbreak of war, that about 6,300 Americans had left Libya by 11 June, and that on 30 August 1967 King Idris criticised Prime Minister Husayn Maaziq’s handling of ‘the riots in June’. One heritage-site page dates the violent demonstrations to 15 June; the other sources point to 5 June. The sources name no street, so the marker is the old city and its Jewish Quarter.

name: Mechiya oasis reprisal, 24–26 October 1911
relevance: Italian troops killed thousands of civilians in the oasis east of Tripoli after the defeat at Shar al-Shatt.
text: Wikipedia’s article on massacres in the Italo-Turkish War says that on the day after the Shar al-Shatt defeat the Italian army attacked the neighbouring Mechiya oasis and over three days killed about 4,000 people, including women and children; the List of massacres in Libya dates it 24–26 October 1911 and says about 100 women and children were burned in a mosque. A contemporary account quoted there says the victims were killed in the streets, in their houses, farms and gardens and, according to a British officer serving with the Turkish forces, in a mosque where several hundred women and children had taken refuge. The Italian war crimes article, citing Duggan, adds that women were raped. Foreign correspondents reported it in detail, and the article says that coverage factored into Britain’s Parliament rejecting a proposed Anglo-Italian Mediterranean agreement. Opposing contemporary arguments, quoted in the same article, called the press reports overblown, so 4,000 is an estimate, not a count. Francesca Di Pasquale writes that an unspecified number of Arabs were shot in the hours after the 23 October revolt and that on 24 October 1911 Prime Minister Giolitti telegraphed the commander in Tripoli ordering the deportation to Italy of all ‘arrested rioters’ (see the unplaced entry on the deportations). Wikipedia places Shar al-Shatt inside the Mechiya oasis, so this marker shares the centre of the Shar al-Shatt marker with a wider 3 km radius; no source gives street-level positions. The main Wikipedia article on the Italo-Turkish War tells the reprisal differently: it says the Italians ‘executed 400 women and 4,000 men through firing squads and hanging in retaliation’ and that Italian authorities used public hangings as retaliation for ambushes. The sources are not reconciled, so whether the dead were killed in a three-day massacre or in part by formal executions is unsettled.

name: Janzur (Zanzur) pogrom, November 1945
relevance: The 1945 anti-Jewish riots spread west from Tripoli to Janzur, where 34 Jews were reported killed.
text: Wikipedia’s article on the 1945 riots gives 34 Jews killed in Zanzur during the riots of 5–7 November 1945, after the violence spread from Tripoli. Its article on Janzur says there was still a Jewish presence there at the end of the Second World War, when a local synagogue was burned down and Jews were killed in a pogrom. Neither says which street or building, and the tolls are Wikipedia’s only count, so the marker is the town centre recorded for Janzur. The Tripoli toll is on the Tripoli pogrom marker.

name: Tajura pogrom, November 1945
relevance: The 1945 anti-Jewish riots also reached Tajura, east of Tripoli.
text: Wikipedia’s article on the 1945 riots says 7 Jews were killed in Tajura during the riots of 5–7 November 1945, after the violence spread from Tripoli. It gives no street, building or other detail, so the marker is the town centre recorded for Tajura.

name: Italian airship bombing at Janzur, 6 March 1912
relevance: Italy used airships to bomb Ottoman and Libyan fighters near Tripoli, said to be the first use of airships in war.
text: Wikipedia’s article on Janzur says that on 6 March 1912 Italian forces became the first to use airships in war, as two dirigibles dropped bombs on Turkish troops and Libyan fighters encamped at Janzour from 6,000 feet. It gives no casualties and cites no other source for the date, so this is a single-source statement. The first aeroplane bombing was near Tajura and Ain Zara on 1 November 1911 (see the unplaced entry). The marker is the town centre recorded for Janzur, with a wide radius because the camp’s position is not given.

name: Two political prisoners die in Abu Salim, July–August 1999
ar: وفاة سجينين سياسيين في سجن أبو سليم، 1999
relevance: Amnesty reported that two political prisoners held in Abu Salim died in custody in mid-1999, with no cause given.
text: Amnesty International’s August 1999 statement marking thirty years of Gaddafi rule says al-Wafi Nbiyya, described as a former ambassador sentenced by the Supreme Military Court in January 1997 over the 1993 army rebellion in Misrata, and Mohammad Ali Bakoush, held without charge or trial since February 1989, both died in Abu Salim prison in Tripoli in July or August 1999. The document does not say which man died in which month, gives no cause of death, and says Amnesty had written to the authorities asking for clarification. It also says five prisoners of conscience convicted in 1973 over the Islamic Liberation Party were reportedly still serving life terms there. The marker is the Abu Salim prison site.

name: Social Welfare Home for Women, Tajoura
relevance: A state ‘social rehabilitation’ home near Tripoli where women and girls were held without charge, visited by Human Rights Watch in 2005.
text: Human Rights Watch researchers visited the Social Welfare Home for Women in Tajoura, near Tripoli, on 4 May 2005 as part of a study of the ‘social rehabilitation’ facilities Libya uses to hold women and girls seen as vulnerable to ‘moral misconduct’. HRW’s report of February 2006 says the home had four solitary-confinement rooms, two of which smelled of paint and one of which had no bathroom, and quotes a woman held there who said she was kept in solitary confinement for a week when she arrived. It says most of the women and girls held in these facilities have no ongoing case and are not serving a criminal sentence, so detaining them without charge, or after a sentence is finished, violates their right to liberty, and it puts the number held in the country’s facilities, this one and a second in Benghazi, at often fewer than one hundred. HRW changed all the names and gives no street address, so the marker is the Tajoura district only. No source seen says when the home opened or closed.

name: Old City (Medina)
summary: The walled historic town on the harbour: Ottoman and Karamanli mosques, souqs, the Red Castle at its eastern corner, and the old Jewish quarters.
history: The street plan is ancient (Roman Oea), but the walls, mosques and souqs mostly date from the Ottoman and Karamanli periods (16th–19th centuries). Landmarks include the Arch of Marcus Aurelius (2nd century AD), the Dragut (Darghut) Mosque near the Bab al-Bahr sea gate (16th century), the Ahmed Pasha Karamanli Mosque (1730s) and the Gurgi Mosque (1830s). The Jewish community lived mainly in two quarters, the Hara Kabira and Hara Saghira, until anti-Jewish riots in 1945, 1948 and 1967 drove almost all of them out of Libya.
era: After 1969 the regime confiscated property left by Jews and Italians. As Tripoli spread outwards, many families left the Old City for newer districts, and its houses were increasingly let to poorer families and, later, migrant workers. Buildings decayed through the 1970s and 1980s. The Red Castle at the Old City’s edge was turned into the national museum. Gaddafi spoke to crowds from the Red Castle ramparts above Green Square on major occasions, including his speech of 25 February 2011.
today: Partly restored but still run-down in places; the souqs remain busy, and in recent years currency dealers have taken over parts of the old markets.
uncertain: Which Old City buildings the security services used in 1969–2011 is not documented in the archive. The OpenStreetMap point “The Turkish Prison” marks the Ottoman-era prison inside the walls.

name: City centre (Italian-era downtown)
summary: The grid of arcaded streets the Italians built south and east of the Old City after 1911, around today’s Martyrs’ Square (Green Square under Gaddafi).
history: Italian Tripoli was built between 1911 and the 1940s: Piazza Italia (later Independence Square, then Green Square, now Martyrs’ Square), the arcaded avenues, the Galleria De Bono, the Catholic cathedral (1923–28) on what became Algeria Square, a theatre and a railway station.
era: After the 1969 coup the square was renamed Green Square and became the regime’s stage for rallies, parades and speeches. In 1970 the cathedral was turned into the Gamal Abdel Nasser Mosque, the year Libya expelled its remaining Italian community and seized their property. Some Italian-era buildings were later demolished, including the Royal Miramare Theatre beside the Red Castle and the central railway station. In February 2011 protesters who tried to gather in Green Square were fired on.
today: Still the commercial heart of the city; the square has been called Martyrs’ Square since August 2011.
uncertain: Dates for individual demolitions under Gaddafi are not in the archive yet.

name: Dahra
summary: Older inner district east of the city centre, between the coast road and Ben Ashour, built up mostly in the Italian period.
era: Dahra lies between the government quarter of the city centre and the embassy district of Ben Ashour; several foreign embassies and Libyan state offices stood in or near it during the Gaddafi era.
today: A dense mixed residential and commercial area close to the centre.
uncertain: The archive does not yet tie specific security offices or arrests to Dahra. Family knowledge of the area would help.

name: Ben Ashour
summary: A well-off residential district south-east of the centre, with villas, embassies and ambassadors’ residences.
era: Under Gaddafi many embassies and diplomats’ homes were here. During the US air raid of 15 April 1986, bombs aimed at Bab al-Aziziya fell instead on homes in this area; houses were destroyed, civilians were killed, and the French embassy nearby was damaged. Libyan officials took foreign journalists to the damaged streets the next morning.
today: Still one of Tripoli’s more affluent districts, with many embassies and offices.
uncertain: Exact streets hit in 1986 and the number of civilian dead in Ben Ashour specifically are not settled in the sources.

name: Fashloum
summary: A dense, older working-class neighbourhood east of the centre, south of Zawiyat al-Dahmani.
era: Fashloum was one of the first Tripoli neighbourhoods to rise against Gaddafi in February 2011; security forces fired on protesters and raided homes there in the days after 20 February 2011.
today: A crowded residential neighbourhood of narrow streets.
uncertain: Its role in earlier opposition, before 2011, is not documented in the archive.

name: Zawiyat al-Dahmani
summary: A coastal district east of the centre, between the sea and Fashloum; formerly the village of Shar al-Shatt.
history: The village of Shar al-Shatt was the scene of the battle and killings of 23–26 October 1911 at the start of the Italian invasion: Ottoman and Libyan fighters overran Italian positions, and Italian troops then killed hundreds of local civilians in reprisal.
era: Part of the inner city under Gaddafi; the 1911 battle was commemorated by the regime as a symbol of resistance to Italy.
today: Residential and commercial; reported under opposition control early in the August 2011 battle for Tripoli.

name: Al-Hani
summary: Eastern inner district between Fashloum and Souq al-Juma; site of the 1911 Battle of Hani (part of the Shar al-Shatt fighting), marked by a memorial.
history: Fighting around al-Hani in late October 1911 was part of the Ottoman–Libyan counter-attack on the Italian lines around Tripoli (the Shar al-Shatt battle). A monument to the Battle of al-Hani stands in the district today.

name: Bab Ben Ghashir
summary: Inner southern district between the city centre and Abu Salim.
uncertain: The archive has no documents tied specifically to this neighbourhood yet.

name: Sidi al-Masri
summary: Inner south-eastern neighbourhood around the Sidi al-Masri shrine and road, between Ben Ashour and Hadba.

name: Ras Hassan
summary: Small inner neighbourhood south of Ben Ashour.

name: Zanata
summary: Eastern neighbourhood between Hadba and Souq al-Juma.

name: Abu Sitta
summary: Coastal area east of the port with the Abu Sitta naval base and an old horse-racing course.
era: The naval base was one of the Libyan navy’s Tripoli facilities under Gaddafi.
today: In March 2016 the UN-backed Presidential Council arrived in Tripoli by sea and set up at the Abu Sitta naval base.

name: Gurji
summary: West-central residential district along the Gurji road, between the centre and Hay al-Andalus.

name: Al-Mansoura
summary: Small inner-west neighbourhood next to Gurji and Bab Akara.

name: Bab Akara
summary: Inner neighbourhood south-west of the centre, close to the northern side of Bab al-Aziziya.

name: Bab al-Aziziya (neighbourhood)
summary: The streets named after the Bab al-Aziziya gate, next to the former Gaddafi compound of the same name.
era: Living beside Gaddafi’s headquarters meant checkpoints, closed roads and a heavy security presence; the area was hit in the 1986 US raid and again by NATO in 2011.

name: Hay Dimashq
summary: Residential neighbourhood between Abu Salim and Hadba.

name: Tekbali camp
summary: Army camp in the Salah al-Din area of southern Tripoli, named after the late Khalifa al-Takbali. On 12 May 2025 the militia leader Abdel Ghani al-Kikli was killed at a meeting here, setting off days of fighting across the city.
era: The camp lies in the belt of army bases south of Salah al-Din that the Gaddafi regime built up around the capital. Its current name, honouring “the late Khalifa al-Takbali”, appears in sources only after 2011, so it was probably known by another name or a number before then.
today: On 1 July 2013 the Third Support Brigade, which had guarded the camp since Gaddafi’s forces were driven from Tripoli, handed it to the national army at a ceremony attended by the head of the General National Congress and the interior minister. By 2025 it was associated with the 444th Brigade: al-Kikli, head of the Stability Support Apparatus, was killed at a meeting at Tekbali camp on 12 May 2025, and his escorts and 444th Brigade guards exchanged fire outside.
uncertain: The camp’s name and units under Gaddafi, and who Khalifa al-Takbali was.

name: Yarmouk camp (32nd Brigade)
summary: Large army base south of Salah al-Din, home of the 32nd Reinforced Brigade — the “Khamis Brigade”, commanded by Gaddafi’s son Khamis.
era: The Khamis Brigade was the regime’s best-armed unit and its main defence of Tripoli in 2011. As the city fell in late August 2011, the bodies of dozens of detainees were found in a burned warehouse near the brigade’s base — the Yarmuk massacre.
today: In the 2019–2020 war Haftar’s forces used Yarmouk as a command centre for the southern Tripoli front; government forces said they retook it on 23 May 2020.

name: Artillery and Missile School
summary: Army artillery and missile training school south of Tripoli, next to the Yarmouk camp; locally “the missiles camp” (al-Sawarikh).
today: Government forces said they retook al-Sawarikh camp from Haftar’s forces on 23 May 2020.
uncertain: Whether the OpenStreetMap “Artillery and Missile School” is the same site news reports call al-Sawarikh camp.

name: Hamza camp
summary: Army camp in southern Tripoli, west of the Yarmouk camp.
today: Government forces said they retook Hamza camp from Haftar’s forces on 23 May 2020.

name: Transport camp
summary: Military transport camp on the southern edge of the city, on the way to the old international airport.

name: 7 April camp
summary: Military camp in south-western Tripoli. Its name recalls 7 April — the date of the 1976 student crackdown and of the public hangings held on that anniversary — a typical Gaddafi-era name.
uncertain: What units used the camp before 2011.

name: Camp 27
summary: Military base west of Janzour, named after kilometre 27 on the coast road west of Tripoli.
today: Fought over repeatedly after 2011, including clashes between the 52nd and 55th brigades for control of the camp.

name: Military College, al-Hadba
summary: Military college in the al-Hadba area of southern Tripoli.
today: On 4 January 2020 an air strike hit cadets gathered on the parade ground, killing about 30 young men aged 18 to 22. The Tripoli government blamed Haftar’s forces, which denied it.

name: Central Security headquarters
aliases: General Administration of Central Security at the Ministry of Interior
الادارة العامة للامن المركزي بوزارة الداخلية
summary: Headquarters of the Interior Ministry’s Central Security force, in the Salah al-Din area.

name: Ghut al-Shaal mobilisation camp
summary: “Tajyeesh” (mobilisation) camp in Ghut al-Shaal. Under Gaddafi, military training was compulsory for secondary-school and university students, and mobilisation centres like this one ran it.
uncertain: Exact dates and use of this camp.

name: Abu Sitta naval base
summary: Navy base on the coast east of the port.
today: The UN-backed Presidential Council landed here by boat on 30 March 2016 and used the base as its first seat in Tripoli.

name: Tajura naval base
summary: Navy base on the coast east of Tajura.

name: Libyan Naval Academy, Janzour (Sidi Bilal)
summary: The navy’s academy on the Janzour coast, by the Sidi Bilal port.
era: On 15 April 1986 US aircraft bombed the Sidi Bilal port facility, which the US said trained naval commandos.

name: Air-defence missile site
summary: A surface-to-air missile site south-east of the city. Under Gaddafi, Tripoli was ringed by Soviet-supplied air-defence missile batteries.
era: A September 1982 CIA imagery report counted more than 70 permanent and field-deployed SAM sites in Libya (SA-2, SA-3, SA-6, SA-9 and Crotale), concentrated around Tripoli, Benghazi and Tobruk. During the US raid of 15 April 1986 Libyan air defences around Tripoli fired heavily; in 2011 NATO struck Libyan air-defence sites in the first days of its campaign.
uncertain: No document we hold gives this exact point, so it is not matched to a dated battery. It sits in the belt of Tripoli-area SAM sites the CIA documented in 1982, which makes a Gaddafi-era battery likely, but the site is not individually dated.

name: 42nd Brigade headquarters
summary: Headquarters of a post-2011 army brigade in the Ain Zara area.

name: 55th Brigade
summary: Base of the 55th Brigade, a post-2011 unit, next to Camp 27 west of Janzour.

name: Al-Ma‘asra
summary: An area marked as military near Gurji in today’s map data; the name means “the press” (as in an olive press).
uncertain: Its history and use are not documented in the archive.

name: Electronic support site
summary: A military area marked “electronic support” south-west of the city.
uncertain: Its history and use are not documented in the archive.

name: Military camp, Tajura
summary: Military camp on the eastern side of Tajura.

name: Mitiga airport (former Wheelus Air Base)
summary: Airport in Souq al-Juma: the Italian Mellaha air base, then the US Wheelus Air Base (1943–1970), then the Libyan Okba Ben Nafi air base; later also used as a civil airport.
era: The US handed Wheelus over on 11 June 1970; it became the Libyan air force’s Okba Ben Nafi base.
today: Tripoli’s only working airport since 2014. The Rada force controls it and runs a prison there; an ICC suspect faces charges over abuses at Mitiga prison in 2014–2020.

name: Tajoura Nuclear Research Centre
aliases: Renewable Energies and Water Desalination Research Centre
summary: Libya’s main nuclear research site, east of Tajura, built with Soviet help around a 10-megawatt research reactor.
era: The reactor began operating in the early 1980s. The centre was part of the nuclear programme Libya renounced in December 2003.
uncertain: The map point is approximate.

name: Red Castle (Assaraya al-Hamra)
summary: The fortress at the corner of the Old City overlooking Martyrs’ (Green) Square, seat of Tripoli’s rulers for centuries and now a museum.
era: Under Gaddafi it housed the national (Jamahiriya) museum. Gaddafi addressed crowds from its ramparts, most famously on 25 February 2011.

name: The Turkish Prison (Old City)
summary: The Ottoman-era prison inside the Old City walls, labelled “The Turkish Prison” in today’s map data.
uncertain: Whether it held prisoners after 1969.

name: Ain Zara prison (“the political prison”)
summary: Prison in Ain Zara that OpenStreetMap labels “the political prison”. The map treats its use for political detainees before 1989 as suspected.
today: Hundreds of inmates escaped during clashes in September 2018.

name: Al-Mabani detention centre
summary: Migrant detention centre in Ghut al-Shaal, opened in 2021 and criticised by the UN and rights groups for overcrowding and abuse.

name: Tripoli Zoo
summary: The city zoo and park in Abu Salim, next to the Bab al-Aziziya compound.
today: In May 2025 the missing-persons authority received reports of mass graves at the zoo, after the Abu Salim fighting.

name: Port of Tripoli
summary: Tripoli’s commercial harbour, north-east of the Old City.
today: Taken by the 444th Brigade in the May 2025 fighting.

name: Former women’s military academy
summary: Former academy of Gaddafi’s female bodyguards (the so-called “Amazons”), between the port and the city centre.
today: Most buildings were demolished around 2017; the site opened as a public park in 2021, keeping only the old gate’s control tower.
uncertain: The map point is approximate (“between the port and the city centre”).

name: Abu Salim
summary: A large, mostly working-class district south of the centre; home to Abu Salim prison, the city zoo and, on its northern edge, the Bab al-Aziziya compound.
era: Abu Salim prison, built inside a military police compound and completed in 1984, became the regime’s main prison for political detainees. On 29 June 1996 about 1,270 prisoners were killed there in what is known as the Abu Salim massacre; families were not told for years, and their protests over it in Benghazi helped spark the 2011 uprising. During the battle for Tripoli in August 2011 Abu Salim was one of the last districts held by Gaddafi loyalists.
today: After 2011 the district was dominated by the Stability Support Apparatus of Abdel Ghani al-Kikli (“Ghnewa”). After he was killed in May 2025 there was heavy fighting in Abu Salim, and the government said it had taken control. In May 2025 more than 50 unidentified bodies were reported in the Abu Salim hospital morgue and the missing-persons authority received reports of mass graves at the zoo.
uncertain: Where in the district the 1996 victims were buried has never been fully established.

name: Hadba al-Khadra
summary: Southern district (“the Green Plateau”) east of Abu Salim, with housing estates, hospitals, the University of Tripoli’s southern faculties and a military college.
era: Mostly built up during the Gaddafi years as the city grew south. The map marks Hadba al-Khadra prison as a suspected site; it is documented as a prison only after 2011.
today: After 2011 al-Hadba prison held senior Gaddafi-era officials, including the former intelligence chief Abdullah al-Senussi and Gaddafi’s son Saadi. On 4 January 2020 an air strike on the military college at al-Hadba killed about 30 cadets.
uncertain: Whether the al-Hadba prison buildings were used for detention before 2011 is not established.

name: Salah al-Din
summary: Southern district with large military camps: Tekbali camp, the Yarmouk camp (once the base of the Khamis Brigade) and other army facilities lie in and around it.
era: Under Gaddafi the area south of Salah al-Din held major army bases. The 32nd Reinforced Brigade, commanded by Gaddafi’s son Khamis and the best-equipped unit in the army, was based at the Yarmouk camp. In late August 2011, as Tripoli fell, the bodies of about 45–50 prisoners were found in a burned warehouse near the brigade’s base: the Yarmuk massacre.
today: The southern camps were front lines in the 2019–2020 war for Tripoli and in the May 2025 clashes, which began with the killing of Abdel Ghani al-Kikli at Tekbali camp.

name: Ain Zara
summary: Large south-eastern district of farms and newer housing; site of a 1911 battle and of a prison long known locally as the political prison.
history: On 4 December 1911 Italian forces attacked the Ottoman–Libyan positions at the Ain Zara oasis in one of the main battles around Tripoli; a memorial stands near the site.
era: Mostly farmland and scattered settlement in the 1970s and 1980s. OpenStreetMap labels the prison here “the political prison – Ain Zara”; the map treats its use for political detainees before 1989 as suspected but not confirmed.
today: Ain Zara prison was badly hit in the clashes of September 2018, when hundreds of inmates escaped. The district was a front line in the 2019–2020 war and was taken by the 444th Brigade in the May 2025 fighting.
uncertain: When the Ain Zara prison was built, and who was held there before 2011.

name: Al-Furnaj (University area)
summary: Eastern-central district around the main campus of the University of Tripoli (called Al-Fateh University under Gaddafi).
era: The university was a centre of student opposition. On 7 April 1976 students at the universities in Tripoli and Benghazi protested against military control and called for elections; the protests were met by violent counter-demonstrations and many students were imprisoned. On 7 April 1977 students were hanged in public in Benghazi; in April 1984 a student was reportedly hanged on the Tripoli campus, and the Washington Post reported on 23 April 1984 on hangings in Tripoli that drew attention to Libyan dissent. Claims of 7 April executions every year into the late 1980s are disputed.
today: Still the main university campus; renamed the University of Tripoli after 2011.
uncertain: Beyond the April 1984 hanging, which executions took place on the Tripoli campus itself still needs confirming.

name: Souq al-Juma
summary: Large eastern district built over old oasis villages and farms; Mitiga airport (the former Wheelus Air Base) lies inside it.
era: Wheelus Air Base, the largest US air base outside the United States in the 1960s, was handed over on 11 June 1970 and renamed Okba Ben Nafi Air Base; the date became the “Evacuation Day” holiday. In February 2011 Souq al-Juma was one of the first districts to rise, and its residents played a leading part in the August 2011 uprising inside Tripoli.
today: Since 2011 the district has been dominated by the Rada (Special Deterrence) force, which runs Mitiga airport and a prison inside it.

name: Tajura
summary: Coastal town east of Tripoli with a 16th-century history, a Soviet-built nuclear research centre and naval and military sites.
history: In 1551 Ottoman forces based at Tajura took Tripoli from the Knights of St John; the Murad Agha Mosque dates from that era.
era: The Tajoura Nuclear Research Centre, with a Soviet-supplied 10-megawatt research reactor, began operating in the early 1980s and was part of Libya’s nuclear programme until it was given up in 2003.
today: On 2 July 2019 an air strike hit the Tajoura migrant detention centre, killing more than 50 people.

name: Janzour
summary: Coastal town on Tripoli’s western edge; the Sidi Bilal port and naval school, bombed in 1986, lie on its shore.
era: The US raid of 15 April 1986 struck the Sidi Bilal port facility, described by the US as a training site for naval commandos. The Libyan naval academy is also in Janzour.
today: A large residential suburb; it saw fighting between armed groups at several points after 2011.

name: Gargaresh
summary: Western coastal district along Gargaresh Road, a long commercial strip of shops and restaurants.
era: Seaside villas and beaches in the Italian and monarchy periods; it grew into a busy suburb under Gaddafi.
today: Home to many migrant workers. On 1 October 2021 security forces raided the district and detained around 5,000 migrants.

name: Hay al-Andalus
summary: Affluent western district of villas and apartment blocks between Gurji and Gargaresh, with several embassies.
era: Largely developed from the 1970s onward as Tripoli expanded west along the coast.

name: Al-Siyahiya
summary: Western coastal district (the name means “the tourist area”) with beaches, hotels and several embassies.

name: Ghut al-Shaal
summary: Western district south of Gargaresh, with an army mobilisation (tajyeesh) camp and, since 2021, the al-Mabani migrant detention centre.
today: Al-Mabani detention centre opened in 2021 and has been criticised by UN agencies and rights groups for overcrowding and abuse.

name: Al-Dribi
summary: Western residential district of villas south of Hay al-Andalus.

name: World Islamic Call Society
summary: Headquarters and college of the World Islamic Call Society, founded under Gaddafi in 1972 to spread Islam abroad.
era: The society trained foreign students and funded mosques and schools across Africa and Asia; it was also a channel for Gaddafi’s foreign influence.

name: Qasr bin Ghashir
summary: Town south of Tripoli next to Tripoli International Airport.
era: The military side of Tripoli International Airport was one of the targets of the US raid of 15 April 1986; Libyan aircraft on the ground were destroyed.
today: Tripoli International Airport was wrecked in the fighting of July–August 2014 and has not reopened; the area was a front line again in 2019–2020.

name: Al-Karimia
summary: South-western outskirts of farms and newer housing on the road to Aziziya.

name: Sawani bin Adam
summary: Southern farming town on Tripoli’s outskirts.

name: Al-Hadba Project
summary: Southern area that grew out of a Gaddafi-era development “project” (mashrou), now largely residential.
uncertain: What kind of project it began as (agricultural or housing) and when.

name: Former shanty neighbourhood (Hay al-Akwakh)
summary: OpenStreetMap labels this area “formerly the huts neighbourhood” — one of the informal settlements on Tripoli’s edge.
uncertain: When the huts were cleared and where residents were moved. Family memory would help here.

name: Rabta chemical plant (Pharma 150)
summary: Reported chemical weapons plant at Rabta, south of Tripoli, publicly presented by Libya as a pharmaceutical factory; subject of the 1990 fire dispute.
history: GlobalSecurity's compilation places the site at Qabilat az Zaribah (Rabta), about 60 miles south of Tripoli. It gives construction as 1984 to 1988. West Germany's intelligence service (BND) and government linked German firm Imhausen Chemie to the project from 1984 onward, and in 1987 the BND judged from satellite images that the plant was most likely for chemical weapons. A November 1988 CIA memo says the Technology Center near Rabta is administratively controlled by the Tajura Nuclear Research Center, that its metal-fabrication section may support the surface-to-surface missile programme, and that it was then probably Libya's most heavily defended site, with SA-2, SA-3, SA-6 and SA-8 units nearby and SA-5s at Al Aziziyah. IAEA GOV/2004/12 Annex II lists a Rabta Engineering Industrial Complex, a Rabta Pharmaceutical Plant and a Rabta Factory 69 bomb-filling plant.
era: The US assessed Rabta in 1990 as the largest chemical weapons plant in the developing world; Libya denied this and claimed a closure that was not confirmed. In March 1990 a fire occurred: Libya blamed the United States, while US officials said satellite imagery showed only minimal damage and called it a hoax; US officials later said production resumed by mid-May 1990. In 1995 Libya reopened it as a pharmaceutical plant, a joint venture with Egypt's Nasr Companies.
today: Libya joined the Chemical Weapons Convention in early 2004. The OPCW stated that Libya declared several chemical weapons production facilities which were destroyed or converted to peaceful uses; the OPCW pages seen do not name Rabta, so its exact post-2004 use is not confirmed here.
uncertain: Three open positions disagree by up to about 7 km, so the pin sits between them with a 6 km radius. (1) The FAS gazetteer lists Qabilat az Zaribah at 32°09′27″N 12°50′32″E. (2) A Google Earth geolocation of 'Ain er Rabta' gives 32°09′51″N 12°51′47″E, 85 km at 202° from Tripoli. (3) OpenStreetMap maps a compound labelled 'Rabta Chemical Weapons Factory' at 32.211°N 12.909°E. Published distances from Tripoli range from about 40 km to 100 km. Treat the pin as the plant area, not a building; no declassified CIA text we hold gives its coordinates.
documented: Assessed by the CIA as a chemical-weapons plant in 1988; declared to the OPCW in 2004

name: Military Police Command compound (reported)
summary: A military police headquarters compound in the Abu Salim district; Abu Salim prison was built inside it.
history: Amnesty International (2006) describes Abu Salim Prison as located in a compound of the Military Police in the area of Abu Salim, a suburb of Tripoli. The Human Rights Solidarity account says it lies within the compound of the Military Police Command and consists of two parallel facilities, the Central Prison and the Military Prison. Published accounts say the prison, completed in 1984, replaced the colonial-era Black Horse prison. During the June 1996 standoff a security team led by Colonel Abdullah al-Senussi, head of military intelligence, arrived and negotiated with the prisoners, so the site was not run by the Military Police alone. By 2005 Human Rights Watch lists Abu Salim among facilities run by the Internal Security Agency. Earlier evidence of the unit: a 1974 CIA National Intelligence Survey says Military Police companies were located in both Tripoli and Benghazi, serving units in their regions. During the May 1984 attack on Bab al-Aziziya, military police surrounded the building where the attackers had retreated, and fighting continued until early afternoon. In March 1988 Gaddafi complained in a speech that military intelligence, the military police and the staff office could each publish lists of people barred from travel (reported by FBIS). In the 2011-era Libyan Army order of battle, a Tripoli Military Police is listed under the Tripoli Military Region.
uncertain: Only the location 'around Abu Salim prison' is supported; the compound's boundaries, buildings and unit structure are not mapped here, so the marker is approximate and wide. The earlier 'police depots' seized in the 1969 coup are not shown to be this compound.

name: Tarhuna (Tarhunah) underground facility
summary: Underground complex in hills near Tarhuna that the US said in 1996 was a chemical weapons plant under construction; Libya denied it.
history: Arms Control Wonk located the site by matching a Defense Department illustration in Google Earth at about 32.473 N, 13.429 E, noting a State Department description of about 60 km southeast of Tripoli. The State Department believed construction began around 1992. Tarhuna town itself lies about 65 km southeast of Tripoli (Wikipedia). The computed distance to the plotted point is about 52 km, so the 60 km figure is approximate.
era: In February 1996 CIA director John Deutch accused Libya of building the world's largest underground chemical weapons plant near Tarhuna. In April 1996 the Defense Intelligence Agency said it was not yet operational, possibly within about a year. Gaddafi said the US photos were faked and described an irrigation project; Egyptian inspectors reportedly saw nothing threatening in late May. In December 1997 the US assessed the facility never became functional and construction had stopped.
today: Present condition is not documented in the pages seen. The 2004 OPCW declaration process did not, in the sources opened, mention this site.
uncertain: Coordinates come from a 2007 blogger's imagery match (Arms Control Wonk), not an official release, so treat as approximate (a few km). The purpose is based on US government claims that Libya disputed; the later US view was that it was never completed.

name: Tripoli Central Hospital
aliases: Vittorio Emanuele III Colonial Hospital (Italian era)
summary: Tripoli's second-largest hospital, founded in the Italian era and home to the city's oldest trauma centre and Libya's organ-transplant programme.
era: Built in 1910 as the Italian colonial Vittorio Emanuele III hospital. It was Tripoli's only trauma centre for the last three decades of the 20th century. Doctors interviewed after the fall of Gaddafi alleged that in February 2011 government troops took over the hospital and that anti-Gaddafi patients were taken away; these are unverified accounts. In October 2011 fighters broke into a sealed section and found a 'secret morgue' with 17 bodies, including a baby, which officials suspected were executed after the 1984 coup attempt. Al Jazeera reported the hospital overwhelmed with casualties on 24 August 2011.
today: Wounded migrants from the July 2019 Tajoura detention-centre air strike were photographed here. Rocket fire around 14 May 2020 partly damaged its communicable-diseases and dermatology buildings, according to the GNA health ministry; the GNA blamed forces loyal to Khalifa Haftar, who denied it. The organ-transplant programme began in 2005, and its outpatient clinics handled about 250,000 cases in 2019.
uncertain: Wikipedia gives coordinates near 32.874, 13.144, about 4 km from the OpenStreetMap hospital polygon used here; the OSM point was preferred. The 'secret morgue' link to 1984 is the suspicion of officials, not a proven finding.

name: Italian Cathedral (Algeria Square / Gamal Abdel Nasser Mosque)
summary: Tripoli's Italian Romanesque Revival cathedral, now a mosque on Algeria Square.
history: Construction began about 1923, with the foundation stone laid that January. It opened in 1928, was consecrated on 24-26 November 1928, and the 60 m bell tower was completed in December 1931. Saffo Panteri designed the basilica with a dome 46 m high. It served a settler population of about 25,000 and was the second Catholic church consecrated in Tripoli, after Santa Maria degli Angeli. A Eucharistic Congress was held in Tripoli on 24 November 1937. A Libyan blog credits Governor De Bono with completing it.
era: In July 1970 the Revolutionary Council confiscated Italian and church property. In September 1970 the Vicar Apostolic of Benghazi was expelled and the cathedral was closed. It became a mosque (Gamal Abdel Nasser Mosque, also Algeria Square Mosque) and the square was renamed Algeria Square. The conversion date is uncertain; the exterior changes were fully visible by about 1998-2000.
today: Open to the public as a mosque. The overall shape and bell tower remain, but the facade and interior were heavily altered. St Francis pro-cathedral is the temporary Catholic cathedral.
uncertain: Exact conversion date. Coordinates from the Wikipedia infobox (32°53'26"N 13°11'9"E).

name: University of Tripoli / Al-Fateh University
summary: Libya's largest university, with more than 45,000 students, based in south-eastern Tripoli.
era: The Tripoli faculties of the University of Libya (Science 1957, Agriculture 1966) became the University of Tripoli in 1973. On 7 April 1976 students in Tripoli and Benghazi protested against military control and demanded elections; security forces suppressed them and many were jailed. The university was renamed Al Fateh University that year. On 7 April 1977 students sentenced by a military tribunal in Tripoli were hanged in public in Benghazi; in April 1984 a student, Rashid Kaabar, was reportedly hanged at the Faculty of Pharmacy on this campus (Washington Post, Asharq Al-Awsat). Claims of hangings every 7 April into the late 1980s are disputed. During the August 2011 Battle of Tripoli the university was the site of a student uprising led by the Students' Union.
today: Renamed the University of Tripoli again in 2012. It runs Medicine, Engineering, Dentistry, Education and many other faculties across several sites, and its teaching hospitals include Tripoli Medical Center, Tripoli Central Hospital, Al-Khadra and Al-Jalaa.
uncertain: The exact spot of the 1984 hanging on campus rests on one account; whether other executions took place on the campus is not confirmed.

name: Ruwagha chemical weapons depot
summary: Remote desert depot in south-eastern Libya where Libya's declared mustard stockpile was stored and destroyed under OPCW monitoring (2010-2014).
history: Libya joined the Chemical Weapons Convention in January 2004 and declared nearly 25 tonnes of bulk mustard agent and thousands of unfilled aerial bombs. The OPCW describes the depot at Ruwagha as being in remote south-eastern Libya, far outside the Tripoli area. Waddan is the nearest town named in the brief.
era: Empty munitions were destroyed in March 2004. Destruction of the bulk mustard began in October 2010 and stopped in February 2011 after equipment failed and unrest began. OPCW inspectors confirmed the stockpile intact in November 2011. Work resumed on 20 April 2013 and ended 4 May 2013; the OPCW announced it on 6 May 2013. Libya completed destruction of its remaining mustard-loaded shells and bombs on 26 January 2014.
today: Precursor chemicals (846 tonnes) remained and were later moved to Germany, completed in 2016-2017 per Wikipedia; the OPCW pages seen cover only the earlier steps. The site's state today is not documented in the pages opened.
uncertain: Position is the Ruwagha (Ar-Rawagha) locality on the edge of Waddan in Al Jufra District, as named on OpenStreetMap, which fits the 'Waddan area' alias and the OPCW's remote-desert description. No source gives the depot's own coordinates and OpenStreetMap shows no military feature there, so the pin marks the named locality with an 8 km radius, not the storage site. Wikipedia also reports rebels finding mustard stocks in Jufra District in 2011; whether that was this depot is not established. Context: a December 1983 CIA imagery board reports 'probable missile-ready bunkers' at Al Jufrah airfield (29.217°N 16.0°E), about 15 km west of this pin; nothing links that airfield to the depot.
documented: Stocks declared in 2004; bulk-mustard destruction completed in 2016-17 (per Wikipedia)

name: Italian Cemetery and Memorial (Hammangi)
summary: The large Italian municipal Christian cemetery and war memorial in the Hammangi/Mansura area, next to the British war cemetery.
history: The Italian municipal Christian cemetery holds the Hammangi memorial, which housed Italian Second World War dead brought to Tripoli under King Idris. The cemetery once held about 15,000 bodies across 12 hectares. The Tripoli War Cemetery is reached through its gate. A separate OpenStreetMap node labelled the "Christian cemetery" lies close by.
era: After the 1970 coup, thousands of remains, including those of Italo Balbo, were repatriated to Italy. The cemetery was left without guards or staff; in 2004 the president of the Italian returnees' association said dogs were among the graves. Ten hectares were returned to the Tripoli municipality, and a first restoration was finished in 2009.
today: After 2011 vandals looted copper and damaged mosaics. A restoration costing about EUR 350,000, designed by Renato Proietti, started in 2019, and the memorial reopened on 7 October 2020 with a Mass. A rocket hit the adjacent British cemetery on 31 May 2020 and grazed the memorial.
uncertain: The cemetery's founding year is not given. Coordinates are OpenStreetMap's "Italian cemetery" area.

name: Mellaha Air Base / Wheelus Air Base / Okba Ben Nafi / Mitiga
ar: قاعدة عقبة بن نافع الجوية / معيتيقة
summary: The Italian airfield that became the huge US Wheelus Air Base and later Tripoli's Mitiga airport.
history: The Italian Air Force built it in 1923 as Mellaha Air Base; the Luftwaffe used it in the North African campaign. The British Eighth Army captured it in January 1943 and US forces used it that month. It became Wheelus Army Air Field on 17 May 1945, named for Lt Richard Wheelus, closed in 1947 and reopened as Wheelus Air Base on 1 June 1948. A 1954 agreement ran to 1971. Its radio station began in 1954 and its TV station on 15 September 1956 was among the first in the Arab world. In 1967-68 King Idris planned to close foreign bases, the largest being Wheelus.
era: Handed to Libya on 11 June 1970 (evacuation completed March 1970 by another count) and renamed Okba Ben Nafi Air Base, it housed the air force headquarters and training, with Soviet aircraft and personnel. The US bombed it on 16 April 1986. In 1995 it became a civilian airport called Mitiga.
today: Since 2018 it has been Tripoli's only international airport; it closed on 8 April 2019 after airstrikes and flights resumed in May 2021.
uncertain: Handover date varies between sources (March vs 11 June 1970). Coordinates are Wikipedia's 32°53'42"N 13°16'49"E and give the airfield centre only.

name: Bin Ghashir tactical missile (Scud and FROG) facility
summary: A probable tactical surface-to-surface missile base south of Tripoli where US imagery analysts counted at least 21 Scud launchers in 1982. This is the only Scud garrison with published coordinates.
history: A 1982 NPIC briefing board gives the coordinates 32°45′30″N 13°12′30″E and reports elements of at least two Scud brigades and one FROG-7 battalion there for the first time: at least 21 Scud MAZ-543 launchers, five resupply semitrailers, two probable FROG-7 launchers and eight FROG-7 resupply vehicles. It suggests the Scuds may have come from the Kulliyat garrison about 6 nautical miles to the north. A December 1980 NPIC report counted at least 59 Scud launchers in six brigades of 9-10 each, deployed or stored at three facilities in the Tripoli area (Tajura South barracks, Madaniyah barracks, and a barracks and vehicle storage depot) and one at Benghazi, with the first Scuds seen at the Al Aziziyah ammunition depot in 1976.
era: Reported 1980-82; whether the base was still used in 2011 is not established.
today: Not described in the documents used.
uncertain: Coordinates are from the CIA briefing board as transcribed in the archive; the page's own distance line ('… nm south of Tripoli') is garbled. This is not the Bab Ben Ghashir district or the Qasr bin Ghashir town, which are on the map separately. The December 1980 report names the other Tripoli-area Scud sites but gives no coordinates for them in the text we hold.
documented: Seen in US imagery in 1982; later use not documented

name: Castel Benito Airfield (Tripoli Idris Airport)
summary: The Italian airfield south of Tripoli that became King Idris's international airport and Tripoli International Airport.
history: A Regia Aeronautica airfield built in 1934 on the southern outskirts of Italian Tripoli. In 1938 Governor Italo Balbo expanded it into a civilian international airport for Ala Littoria, with routes to Rome, Tunis and Malta. The British Eighth Army captured it in January 1943, after Allied raids had destroyed it; three days later a BOAC Lockheed 14 landed there. The Royal Engineers built three runways that year. After independence in 1951 it was renamed Idris el Awal (Idris I) and was the only thing named after the king.
era: After the 1969 revolution it was renamed Tripoli International Airport. A new 09/27 runway started in 1966 was completed later, and a new terminal opened on 28 July 1978. Wikipedia does not name Gaddafi in its account of the airport.
today: Fighting from 14 July to 23 August 2014 destroyed at least 90 percent of its facilities and 20 aircraft; passenger flights moved to Mitiga.
uncertain: Whether the Castel Benito name predates 1934 is unknown. Coordinates are from the Wikipedia infobox.

name: Al Fateh Tower (Tripoli Tower)
summary: A tall mixed-use tower on the Corniche (Gulf Street) near the central business district, known as Al Fateh Tower and now as Tripoli Tower. It holds shops, serviced apartments and a small hotel, and is a separate building from Fateh University.
era: Wikipedia lists it as opening in 2003 in the infobox, while its article text says 1999. It was called Al Fateh Tower before it became Tripoli Tower. Reported height is 112 to 120 metres and 25 to 28 floors (the page contradicts itself). It has four basement car-parking levels. It is a different building from the Corinthia Hotel complex and from the That El Emad Towers, which stand nearby. The sources seen contain no specific events at the tower during 1969-2011.
today: A Libya Monitor report dated 24 July 2013 says a rocket hit a residential tower in the main business area near Tripoli Tower (formerly Burj al-Fateh); the report did not name the building hit and no injuries were reported. The tower's present condition is not described in the sources seen.
uncertain: Two heights, two floor counts and two opening years are given. Architect, owner and the date of the renaming from Al Fateh Tower to Tripoli Tower are not stated. The coordinate comes from Wikipedia's infobox only. Check whether the 'Fateh Towers' twin-tower description from the owner matches this single tower.

name: Tripoli International Airport
summary: Tripoli's former main airport south of the city, built by the Italians in 1934, largely destroyed in 2014 and under reconstruction.
era: Built in 1934 as Tripoli-Castel Benito, renamed Idris el Awal in 1951 and given its present name after 1969. A new terminal opened on 28 July 1978. In 2007 a 2.1 billion dollar expansion with two new terminals was contracted, but work was halted by the 2011 war. The airport was closed from March to October 2011, captured by the Zintan brigade on 21 August 2011, and reopened on 11 October 2011.
today: Misratan militias attacked on 14 July 2014; after about 40 days of fighting Zintan forces withdrew, and the LA Times reported at least 90 per cent of facilities and 20 aircraft destroyed. Flights moved to Mitiga. The Libyan National Army held it from April 2019 to June 2020. Reconstruction of two terminals began in February 2023; the contract was revoked in 2024 and a new contractor was appointed in July 2025. Opening is scheduled for the fourth quarter of 2026.
uncertain: Sources conflict on whether limited flights resumed in 2017. The coordinate is the centre of the large OSM airport area.

name: Royal Palace of Tripoli (Qasr al-Khuld) / Italian Governor's Palace
summary: A large palace built for the Italian governors of Tripolitania, later the monarch's Tripoli residence, then a public library.
history: Built in 1924-1931 during Italian rule to a design by Saul Meraviglia Mantegazza, as the residence of the colonial governors of Italian Tripolitania. A Libyan blog says Governor De Bono, in office from 1925, completed the Governor's Palace; Wikipedia's timeline gives 1929. It later became the residence of the Libyan monarch in Tripoli. A palace-secretary memoir says the Tripoli palace hosted routine visits and that the royal palaces were modest villas. Independence Street leads from Independence Square to King Idris's palace.
era: After Colonel Gaddafi's 1969 coup the palace was converted into a public library, ending its use as a royal residence. The Wikipedia page gives no further detail on its use during the Gaddafi period or on any changes to the building.
today: What the building is used for now was not stated. Coordinates are from the Wikipedia infobox.
uncertain: Which monarch lived there is not stated. A Royal Palace "in Gargaresh" and a separate "Government Palace" were not found in any source; it may be the same building. A Libyan Museum building appears near these coordinates in OpenStreetMap but was not matched.

name: Martyrs' Square (formerly Green Square)
summary: Tripoli's main public square beside the Red Castle and the waterfront. It was Piazza Italia under the Italians, Green Square under Gaddafi, and was renamed Martyrs' Square by rebels in 2011.
era: The Italians built it on the site of an old bread market and called it Piazza Italia; it was enlarged in the 1930s. It was Independence Square from 1951 to 1969, then renamed Green Square after the 1969 revolution to reflect the Green Book. The Royal Miramare Theatre opposite the Red Castle was demolished by Gaddafi's government to make room for large rallies. In February 2011 protesters filled the square in a failed uprising, and pro-Gaddafi rallies followed.
today: Rebels took the square on the night of 21-22 August 2011 and renamed it Martyrs' Square. Tens of thousands celebrated there on 31 August and 2 September 2011. A militia group rallied there around 5 November 2016. The square, with a large central fountain, remains a main downtown tourist attraction and commercial centre.
uncertain: Exact dates of the demolition of the Miramare Theatre are not given.

name: Radisson Blu Al Mahary Hotel
summary: A city-centre hotel on Elfatah Street that stands on the site of the Italian-era Hotel del Mehari. Since 2016 it has also served as a meeting place for Libya's High Council of State.
era: The Italian Hotel del Mehari was built in 1935, designed by Florestano Di Fausto with Stefano Gatti-Casazza. The present hotel opened in 1989 and was fully remodelled in 2009 to international standards under the Radisson name. After the 2011 war began it closed briefly, then reopened a few months later under local management. In 2012 Carlson Rezidor (now the Radisson Hotel Group) returned as operator. The sources seen do not describe how it was used under Gaddafi.
today: The High Council of State met here on 27 February 2016 and was formally established here on 5 April 2016. It moved to the Rixos Al Nasr complex on 22 April 2016, and returned to the Radisson in October 2016 after fighting there. As of 2026 Wikipedia calls it one of only two international chain hotels in Libya.
uncertain: It is not documented who ran the hotel in 1989-2009 or what happened there in 2011 beyond the brief closure.

name: Jarmah missile launch site (OTRAG), later used for Libyan missile development
summary: The German OTRAG rocket range in the Libyan desert, about 380 nautical miles south of Tripoli. By December 1983 CIA imagery said the Libyans were using it to develop a short-range missile.
history: A March 1981 NPIC report describes a fenced site about 2 by 1 km with a 19 m lattice launch tower, propellant storage, 16 prefabricated housing units, workshops, a water reservoir and a 2,370 m runway, built by the West German firm OTRAG after its Zaire range was cancelled in 1979. An August 1982 board records a new concrete launch pad at coordinates 26°33′05″N 13°09′50″E. OTRAG ended its Libyan launch work in December 1981 and left in 1981-82 (Aviation Week; Der Spiegel). A December 1983 board shows a launch in preparation with a crane over the erector-launcher and says the site was 'currently being used by the Libyans for the development of a short-range missile'.
era: 1980-1983; later use is not documented in the sources held.
today: Not described in the documents used.
uncertain: Coordinates are from the CIA briefing boards of 1982 and 1983. Their text says the site is '5.5 nm east of Jarmah', which does not fit the town of Jarma (Germa) on modern maps, so the coordinates are used and the place name is not. Wikipedia places OTRAG's Libyan centre at Tawiwa near Sabha (26.99°N 14.46°E), and GlobalSecurity says a March 1981 test came 'from either the Sebha Oasis or the Jarmah Oasis'; the CIA imagery supports the Jarmah site. Which later Libyan missile programme used it is not stated.
documented: Imagery 1981-83; OTRAG left in 1981-82; later use not documented

name: Jewish Cemetery of Tripoli
summary: The main Jewish burial ground of Tripoli, on the coast west of the city, largely built over after 1969.
history: A 1943 photograph shows Allied soldiers surveying the cemetery after the Germans had used many of its gravestones for coastal defences as the Eighth Army advanced. It lay on the coast just west of Tripoli. OpenStreetMap maps an "Old Jews Graveyard" next to the Italian cemetery and Tripoli War Cemetery in the Hammangi area. Libya's Jewish population fell from about 40,000 in World War II to about 100 by 1969.
era: In 2002 David Gerbi found children playing among debris with human remains. By 2007 he found the debris cleared, a highway built over the site and a high-rise on it. An Israeli news interview with Meir Kachlon claims Gaddafi crushed the graves and dumped them in the sea, and that the area was built over. These accounts are not independently verified.
today: A virtual cemetery project was announced to replace the destroyed Jewish cemeteries.
uncertain: How the OpenStreetMap graveyard relates to the larger cemetery described in news reports is unknown. Kachlon gives 130 acres, unconfirmed. When it was destroyed is not dated. Founding date unknown.

name: Mitiga (Okba Ben Nafi) air base
ar: قاعدة عقبة بن نافع الجوية / مطار معيتيقة
summary: Former Wheelus Air Base and Libyan Air Force base east of Tripoli, struck by US aircraft on 15-16 April 1986.
history: Founded by Italy in 1923 as Mellaha, later used by the Luftwaffe, the British and then US forces as Wheelus. US forces left by 1970 after the 1969 coup, and it became the Libyan air base Okba Ben Nafi, with Soviet aircraft and personnel also based there.
era: Early on 15 April 1986 five US F-111s bombed the airfield, destroying two Il-76 transports, according to the account cited on Wikipedia. It was one of the five targets in Operation El Dorado Canyon, the others being Bab al-Azizia, Murat Sidi Bilal, and two sites at Benghazi. One F-111F was lost during the overall raid, according to Wikipedia's airport page.
today: It became a civil airport in 1995 and is mixed civil and military. Since 2018 it has been Tripoli's only international airport after Tripoli International was damaged in 2014-2019 fighting. Runways are 3,376 m and 1,829 m.
uncertain: Coordinates are the OpenStreetMap outline (the project data). Dates in sources vary between 15 and 16 April depending on time zone.

name: Sebha airfield
summary: The air base at Sebha, where US imagery recorded MiG-25 Foxbat interceptors in 1982 and resupply flights to Chadian dissidents in 1983.
history: Jan 1982: Foxbat high speed, high altitude interceptor and reconnaissance aircraft have deployed to Sebha airfield. this is the first identification of Foxbat at this airfield. May 1982: The Libyan air force has recently lost a probable Mirage iii/v and a possible Fitter in two separate crashes. oe (s/d). May 1982: The Libyan air force has recently lost a probable Mirage iii/v and a possible Fitter in two separate crashes. Dec 1982: Four Foxbat a high altitude fighter/intercepter aircraft have been armed with acrid ‘aa-6) air-to-air missiles. Libyan Foxbat normally are ot observed armed. Aug 1983: Resupply efforts to Libyan-backed Chadian dissident forces continue.
era: Documented in declassified CIA imagery reports dated 1982–1983, so it was in Gaddafi-era use then.
today: Not described in the documents used.
uncertain: Coordinates are those printed in the CIA briefing boards. The reports date only what the imagery showed; when the site was built, how long it stayed in use and who used it after 2011 are not documented here.
documented: Seen in US imagery in Jan 1982 and Aug 1983; later use not documented

name: Karamanli House Museum (Harem of Ali Karamanli)
summary: A two-storey 18th-century Karamanli house in the Old City, now a small museum of domestic life.
history: Built in the second half of the 18th century during the reign of Ali Pasha Karamanli (1754-1793). It was first known as the Harem House, and Yusuf Pasha is said to have lived there until his death. In the second Ottoman period (after 1835) a consulate, called "Tuscania" on the source page, was based in it. The two-storey house has a fountain and mosaic-covered walls, four rooms and a kitchen downstairs, and costumes, furniture and a weapons room above.
era: The Old City Project restored it in the early 1990s and it was officially opened on 27 October 1994 as the "Tripoli Historical Exhibition". It displays furniture, copper and brass, clothing, jewellery and early gadgets such as a gramophone, a telephone and a radio.
today: Operating status is not confirmed; the page quoting entrance fees may be out of date.
uncertain: The page gives two slightly different restoration dates. The OpenStreetMap point is labelled "The Harem of Ali Garamanli". Whether "Tuscania" is a correct consulate name is unclear.

name: Corinthia Hotel Tripoli (Corinthia Bab Africa)
summary: A twin-tower hotel complex on the Tripoli waterfront, opened in 2003 and described as the largest hotel in Libya. It is operated by Corinthia Hotels International.
era: Opened in 2003 in the central business district; Wikipedia says it was opened by Prime Minister Shukri Ghanem, but that claim is marked 'citation needed'. Tower 1 has 28 floors and tower 2 has 14; the hotel has 319 rooms and four restaurants. It stands 120 m high. The sources seen contain no specific events at the hotel during the Gaddafi era or the 2011 war.
today: On 27 January 2015 gunmen attacked the hotel and killed ten people, including five foreigners and an American security contractor. Islamic State in Tripoli Province claimed responsibility. Before the main attack a car bomb injured six people nearby. Wikipedia (2026) names it one of only two international chain hotels in Libya, the other being the Radisson Blu Al Mahary.
uncertain: Gaddafi-era use and 2011 events are not documented in the sources seen. One news source gives a toll of nine rather than ten for the 2015 attack. Opening ceremony claim is unsourced.

name: Janzour (reported centrifuge machine shop site)
summary: Western suburb of Tripoli named in IAEA-based summaries as the site of a machine shop used by the undeclared nuclear programme.
history: Janzour lies west of central Tripoli, in the Tripoli built-up area and east of the town of Az-Zawiya. NTI's summary of IAEA findings lists a Janzour machine shop for centrifuge-related manufacturing, one of the undeclared sites Libya disclosed in 2003-04.
era: Reported in IAEA-based and Western accounts after Libya's December 2003 announcement as part of the undeclared nuclear programme, which Libya said it had run without notifying the IAEA. The programme's equipment was removed under US, UK and IAEA supervision in three stages, completed in September 2004, according to the Nuclear Threat Initiative's summary.
today: The pages seen do not describe the facility's current state. The area is an ordinary suburb with housing and businesses.
uncertain: Coordinates are the Janzour town centre from Wikipedia (about 32.817 N, 13.011 E); the actual workshop address is not published in the pages seen. Location approximate (several km).

name: Al-Razi Psychiatric Hospital
summary: Tripoli's psychiatric hospital, described as the only mental hospital serving western, central and southern Libya.
era: It opened about three decades before a 2019 article describing it, with roughly 200 beds, and treated 60 to 70 percent of Libya's mental-health service users. Reports say it received less funding and attention under Gaddafi, with poorly maintained buildings and little rehabilitation. During the August 2011 fighting a patient escaped, guards left, and inpatients were frightened by NATO bombing.
today: After Tripoli fell, new management introduced reforms within six months: a 40-bed rehabilitation unit, a 16-bed subacute unit, a renovated 40-bed acute unit with international-standard seclusion rooms, CCTV and an outpatient department, with 23 new doctors and 50 new nurses recruited. In late 2011 it reported shortages of staff and medicine.
uncertain: Exact opening year not stated.

name: Murat Sidi Bilal naval commando camp
summary: Coastal camp west of Tripoli bombed by the US in April 1986, described by the US as a naval commando and frogmen training site.
history: Wikipedia's account of the 1986 raid places the Murat Sidi Bilal camp in the Tripoli area. OpenStreetMap maps a Sidi Bilal mosque at 32.821 N, 12.957 E and a Libyan naval academy nearby, which the project uses as the locator.
era: On 15 April 1986 all three F-111s assigned to this camp bombed it, according to the account of the raid cited on Wikipedia. The US described the camp as a training site for naval commandos and combat frogmen, in the context of reprisals for the 5 April 1986 Berlin discotheque bombing.
today: Not documented in the sources seen. The site lies in the western coastal area of Greater Tripoli, near built-up land and the naval academy mapped in OpenStreetMap, but its current use was not checked.
uncertain: Location approximate: the point is a nearby mosque in OpenStreetMap, not the camp boundary. The camp's exact extent was not found. The US purpose description is the US government's, and Libya disputed civilian-versus-military framing.

name: Janzur (Zanzur) and Italian Giorgimpopoli
summary: A coastal town west of Tripoli, site of the 1912 battles and of an Italian-period settlement.
history: First settled in the 6th century BC. It was a district of the Ottoman sanjak of Tripoli; in 1862 it was split into Janzour and Al-Aziziya. On 6 March 1912 Italian airships bombed Turkish troops and Libyan fighters camped at Janzour, the first use of airships in war, according to a New York Times report of 8 March. A Jewish community lived there until the end of World War II, when a local synagogue was burned and Jews were killed in the November 1945 pogrom. Under the Kingdom it belonged to the Tripoli governorate.
era: It became a municipality in 1983 and was later reassigned between districts: Tripoli in 1995, Zawia in 1998 and Al-Jafara in 2001. It now hosts the Libyan Academy and some faculties of the University of Tripoli.
uncertain: The name Giorgimpopoli, mentioned in the request, is not in the sources opened, so the link is not confirmed. Coordinates are the Wikipedia town centre.

name: Abu Salim Prison
summary: A maximum-security prison in south Tripoli, built in 1984 and the scene of the June 1996 massacre.
era: Built by foreign workers in 1984 from prefabricated slabs, with a military and a central block; the first prisoners arrived in September 1984 after the Bab al-Azizia coup attempt. On 28-29 June 1996, after a protest over food, guards killed prisoners in the courtyards; Human Rights Watch estimated over 1,200 dead. Gaddafi admitted the killings in 2004 after eight years of denial.
today: Rebels captured it on 24 August 2011 and freed prisoners, though loyalist troops fired on some. A reported mass grave announced on 25 September 2011 turned out to hold what looked like animal bones. On 2 May 2021 Libya's Supreme Court ruled the massacre a genocide and sent the case back to a lower court. Current use was not stated.
uncertain: The death toll is an estimate.

name: Arch of Marcus Aurelius
summary: The best-preserved Roman monument of ancient Oea, a four-faced marble triumphal arch at the edge of the Old City.
history: Built in 165 AD by Gaius Calpurnius Celsus, a magistrate of Oea, to mark Lucius Verus's victories over the Parthians (161-66). It is a four-faced marble arch with an unusual octagonal dome; Apollo and Minerva, the city's patron gods, appear on the pediments. It was partly buried over the centuries. Statues of the emperor and Verus were recovered in 19th-century digs, and the four niches are now empty. The Italian administration did conservation work in 1914-1918, and the architect Florestano Di Fausto reorganised the surroundings in the 1930s. It was only slightly damaged in World War II.
today: As of 2017 it suffered from poor upkeep, visitor damage and acid rain wearing away its carved detail.
uncertain: Wikipedia gives 165 AD and says it was built at Oea. A travel-site page (Temehu) says 163 AD and that it was moved from Leptis Magna; that claim is not supported elsewhere in the sources opened. Nothing was found on its Gaddafi-era treatment. Coordinates are from OpenStreetMap.

name: Gazelle Fountain (Gazelle and the Beauty)
summary: A bronze Italian fountain of a seated woman and a gazelle on the Corniche, a symbol of Tripoli.
history: Designed by the Italian sculptor Angiolo Vannetti in 1932, originally named "Sorgente di Vita" (Source of Life). It shows a nude woman on a rock embracing a gazelle, set in water, facing the sea. Historian David Rifkind reads the woman as Italy and the gazelle as Tripolitania and Cyrenaica, united in 1934. Vannetti said the work expressed the city, the gazelle the desert and the woman the sea.
era: Gaddafi spared it, along with two harbour columns topped by Romulus and Remus, even while removing other Italian monuments. The 1970s road works filled in the sea in front of it.
today: Cleaned in 2012; wrapped in blue cloth in 2012, hit by an RPG in 2013, and removed in 2014. In February 2021 a plain fountain replaced it.
uncertain: The coordinates are OpenStreetMap's "Statue Belle and Spinner" point, a mislabelled English name for the gazelle statue. Where the statue was kept after 2014 is not stated.

name: Abu Salim Trauma Hospital
summary: A four-storey trauma hospital in the Abu Salim district, the site of one of the worst scenes of the 2011 Battle of Tripoli.
era: On 25 August 2011 MSF found dozens of bodies in the compound and 22 patients and five staff trapped by fighting; the two most critical patients were moved to Tripoli Medical Centre. Reporters on 26 August found about 41 decomposing bodies (21 in one room, 20 in the courtyard); MSF reported over 200, and Airwars records estimates between 39 and 200. Pro-Gaddafi snipers were reported to have used the building until rebels secured it. In the 13 November 2013 Gharghour shootings, Human Rights Watch named Abu Salim Trauma Hospital as one of the hospitals that received the wounded; officials counted 43 dead and 460 wounded in all.
today: No post-2013 hospital-specific events were found.
uncertain: How and when the 2011 victims died is not established by the sources; reports describe both rebels and loyalists among them.

name: Tripoli War Cemetery (Commonwealth)
summary: The Commonwealth war graves cemetery for the Second World War, entered through the old Italian cemetery.
history: Montgomery's Eighth Army captured Tripoli on 23 January 1943, after which the city became a hospital centre. Burials came almost entirely from hospitals, including No. 2, No. 48 and No. 133 General Hospitals from March 1943 and No. 89 General Hospital from April 1944. There are 1,369 Commonwealth Second World War burials, 133 of them unidentified, plus 19 non-Commonwealth and 7 non-war-service burials. It lies in the Mansura district, about 2.5 km west of the centre, off the west end of Sharia Jamahuriya.
today: The Commission planned a renovation of several Libyan cemeteries because the climate has eroded headstones. A rocket fell on the adjacent British cemetery on 31 May 2020.
uncertain: The founding date is not given. The Gaddafi-era upkeep is not documented in the sources opened. Coordinates are from the ww2cemeteries page.

name: Tarabulus port facilities (military deliveries)
summary: Tripoli harbour as the US imagery watched it: Soviet arms deliveries, including SA-2 missile components, arrived here in 1982.
history: Apr 1982: An Iranian merchant ship and cargo aircraft in Libya suggests ccntinued Libyan military support to Iran. Oct 1982: Libya has received a shipment of Soviet arms, including components for at least two SA-2 surface-to-air missile batteries. Dec 1982: Additional Soviet arms have been delivered to Libya. Feb 1983: Arms transshipment activity is observed at this port. Feb 1983: An arms delivery has occurred since and transshipment activity involving SA-2 surface to air missile (sam) equipment continues.
era: Documented in declassified CIA imagery reports dated 1982–1983, so it was in Gaddafi-era use then.
today: Not described in the documents used.
