uncertain: Coordinates are those printed in the CIA briefing boards. The reports date only what the imagery showed; when the site was built, how long it stayed in use and who used it after 2011 are not documented here.
documented: Seen in US imagery in Apr 1982 and Feb 1983; later use not documented

name: Al Jufrah airfield
summary: An airfield at Al Jufrah, reportedly built by the Soviets, that US imagery said had become operational for advanced jets by December 1983, with six probable missile-ready bunkers.
history: Dec 1983: Al jufrah airfield, reportedly being constructed by the soviets, has become an operational, advanced, jet-capable airfield. 2g. name: Dragut (Sidi Darghut) Mosque and tomb
summary: The first Ottoman-style mosque in Tripoli, built after the 1551 conquest and holding the tomb of the commander Dragut.
history: Built around 1560 on the site of a Hospitaller church, which local tradition says was kept inside the mosque. Dragut died at the 1565 Siege of Malta and was buried here with his family. Iskander Pasha altered it in the early 1600s and rebuilt the minaret in 1602. Monument surveyors visited in 1921 and it was restored in the 1920s. Bombing in World War II badly damaged the central part. Ali Mohamed Abu Zaian led the rebuilding, which differs from the original; the domes rose from 27 to 32. One account dates the restoration to 1946.
today: Still a mosque; in 2014 armed men tried several times to vandalise it and were repelled.
uncertain: Sources give the construction year as 1556, about 1560 or 1565. Nothing was found on the Gaddafi period. Coordinates are from the Wikipedia infobox.

name: British Embassy, Tripoli
summary: The UK diplomatic mission in Tripoli, besieged in 1984, burned in 2011 and reopened in October 2011.
era: After gunfire from the Libyan People's Bureau in London killed WPC Yvonne Fletcher on 17 April 1984, Britain broke relations on 22 April. In Tripoli about 60 Revolutionary Guards surrounded the British embassy, trapping its staff including Ambassador Oliver Miles, until the siege was lifted. Relations were restored after Libya accepted responsibility in 1999 and were normalised by 2007. On 1 May 2011 a mob burned the embassy and ambassador's residence after a NATO strike, leaving 'burned shells'.
today: William Hague reopened the embassy on 17 October 2011 and appointed Sir John Jenkins ambassador. Its status since then was not found.
uncertain: The OSM point may be a later location; the building burned in 2011 may have been elsewhere. Wikipedia's page gives the 1984 lift date as 18 April.

name: Al-Khadra General Hospital
summary: One of Tripoli's biggest public hospitals and a teaching hospital of the University of Tripoli, heavily used in the 2019-2020 war.
today: Its emergency wing saw more than 250,000 patients in 2019. After a 4 January 2020 air strike on a military school it treated 33 wounded in one night and received 30 bodies. It was built for about 300 emergency cases at a time but sometimes saw 3,000 patients a day, with about a third of the care staff it needed. On 6 April 2020, while it was the city's only dedicated COVID-19 hospital, projectiles hit its grounds and wounded at least six health workers; the Abu Salim council blamed Libyan National Army rockets and the UN called it a clear violation of humanitarian law.
uncertain: Gaddafi-era history was not found in the sources consulted.

name: Al Hashan (Site A), Libya's first centrifuge site
summary: Libya's first gas-centrifuge research and development site, active 1997-2002 on the outskirts of Tripoli; the pin marks Ain Zara, where an 'Al Hashan Street' is recorded.
history: IAEA GOV/2004/12 Annex I lists it as 'Site A: the original centrifuge R&D location (Al Hashan)'. Paragraphs 22-23: Libya installed a single complete centrifuge there in 2000 and later a larger hall; the equipment was moved to Al Fallah (Site B).
era: Libya moved the equipment to Al Fallah (Site B) by April 2002 and the programme later centred on Al Khalla. The site was declared in 2003-04 and the US, UK and IAEA removed all nuclear equipment by September 2004.
today: Not described in the pages seen. No weapons material is reported to remain.
uncertain: The IAEA names the site 'Al Hashan' but gives no suburb, street or coordinates (GOV/2004/12 contains no distances or addresses). The pin is Ain Zara, from GlobalSecurity ('outskirts of Tripoli') and an 'Al Hashan Street' registry address, so it is suburb-level. A 1982 Libyan grain-silo plan also lists an 'al-Hashshan silo' (JPRS 2655), which is probably unrelated.
documented: Centrifuge work 1997-2002 (IAEA); cleared 2004

name: Grand Hotel Tripoli
summary: A hotel overlooking the harbour near Martyrs' Square. The Italian Grand Hotel (1927) was demolished in the early 1980s and a new hotel was built on the site in 1982.
era: The first Grand Hotel was built by the Italians in 1927 in a Moorish-revival style and hosted General Rommel in 1941. It was heavily bombed in 1942 but kept operating until it was demolished in the early 1980s. The replacement hotel was designed by the British firm Wakeman Trower and Partners and built in 1982. The sources seen do not say why the older building was demolished.
today: The hotel closed in 2011 because of the civil war. It is defunct, but plans for renovation and reopening were announced in December 2025.
uncertain: Reason for the demolition is not documented. Whether anything happened at the hotel in 2011 beyond the closure is not stated.

name: Tripoli International Stadium (11 June Stadium)
summary: Libya's national stadium, a 50,000-seat venue in western Tripoli.
era: Named 11 June after the date in 1970 when US forces left Libya's Wheelus base. Wikipedia says it opened in 1970 while another timeline lists 1982. It hosted many matches of the 1982 African Cup of Nations, including the Ghana v Libya final, and the 2002 Italian Supercup (Juventus 2-1 Parma).
today: Renamed after 2011. A renovation was completed on 8 March 2024, reopening with a Milan All-Stars v Libya All-Stars match before over 50,000 fans. In 2025 Al-Ahly Tripoli and Al-Ittihad drew full 50,000 crowds there for CAF Champions League games. It is shared by the national team, Al-Ittihad, Al-Ahli Tripoli and Al-Madina.
uncertain: Sources disagree on the opening year (1970 vs 1982).

name: Tripoli Medical Center
summary: Tripoli's largest public hospital and the main teaching hospital of the University of Tripoli medical faculty.
era: A Libyan-government-funded training project with the Medical University of Vienna ran at the hospital from 2006 (first assessments April 2006, training from spring 2007), when it was described as a 1,300-bed public hospital with over 3,000 staff. In the 2011 Battle of Tripoli, Medecins Sans Frontieres evacuated its two most critical patients from Abu Salim hospital to the Tripoli Medical Centre on 25 August 2011 and planned to assess its needs two days later.
today: It remains one of Tripoli's main referral hospitals and a teaching hospital of the University of Tripoli.
uncertain: Opening date not found. Bed and staff figures are from a Vienna university project page that may be dated.

name: Naqa (Al-Naqah) Mosque
summary: Probably the oldest Islamic monument in Tripoli, rebuilt in 1610-11 and reusing Roman and Byzantine columns.
history: Its early history is poorly documented. It was most likely first built in 973 under the Fatimid caliph al-Mu'izz. Two legends explain the name "Mosque of the Camel", both involving a gold-laden camel. It was badly damaged or destroyed during the Spanish occupation in the 16th century. An inscription records rebuilding in 1610-11 by the Ottoman-era governor Safar Dey. The prayer hall has 36 columns, including reused Roman and Byzantine ones, and 42 domes. The floor now lies about 0.4 m below street level.
today: An active mosque. Coordinates are from the Wikipedia infobox.
uncertain: The 973 date is a probable one only. Nothing on Gaddafi-era use or recent restoration was found.

name: Libyan Academy for Postgraduate Studies (Academy of Graduate Studies)
summary: Libya's postgraduate institution in Tripoli, set up in 1988 as an economics institute.
era: Founded in 1988 as the Graduate Institute of Economic Sciences, it began graduate teaching in autumn 1989 with accounting, management and economics. In 1995 Decision No. 996 renamed it the Academy of Graduate Studies and let it award graduate diplomas and master's degrees. It later grew to eight schools including engineering, languages, strategic studies and medical sciences.
today: Under Council of Ministers Resolution No. 167 of 2012 it became the Libyan Academy, under the Ministry of Higher Education and Scientific Research, offering postgraduate teaching, consulting and research training.
uncertain: The OSM mapping is on the western edge of the city near Janzour; the academy has other sites.

name: Uaddan Hotel and Casino (Al Waddan Hotel)
summary: A glamorous Italian-era seafront hotel with a casino and theatre, later restored as a luxury hotel.
history: Built in 1935 (opened 1936) as the Italian Uaddan Hotel and Casino, alongside the Hotel Al Mehari. The architect was Florestano Di Fausto, working with Stefano Gatti-Casazza. It had a casino and a 500-seat theatre. An American journalist called it "the Waldorf Astoria of Tripoli" and it has been described as a jewel of modern African architecture. Wikipedia places the Grand Hotel just to its west.
today: Fully restored between 2007 and 2009 at about $16 million as an international luxury hotel, managed for several years by InterContinental. Coordinates from the Wikipedia infobox.
uncertain: The infobox says 1935 and the text says 1936 for the opening. Current operating status after 2011 was not found.

name: Shar al-Shatt (Sciara Sciat) battlefield
summary: The eastern oasis district of Tripoli where Ottoman and Arab forces attacked the Italians on 23-26 October 1911.
history: The battle took place 23-26 October 1911 on the outskirts of Tripoli. Ottoman and Arab forces attacked the thinly fortified eastern sector, held by the 11th Bersaglieri, firing from the oasis and houses. The 4th Company barricaded itself in a cemetery and surrendered; about 290 surrendered soldiers were killed. Italian official losses were 503 dead and 158 wounded. The Italians retook the area on the evening of 23 October. Harsh reprisals followed on 24 October, and one account says thousands of civilians died and a mosque with 100 refugees inside was burned.
uncertain: Casualty figures vary widely between and within sources. Wikipedia's coordinates give the battle area only, not a specific site. A Bersaglieri monument at Porta Pia in Rome commemorates it.

name: Old British Consulate (Karamanli-era house)
summary: A decorated courtyard house built by the Karamanli family in 1744 and once the residence of the British consul.
history: Built by the Karamanli family in 1744 and used as the residence of the British Consul. A small doorway off Shar'a al-Kuwash opens onto a large decorated courtyard, according to Philip Ward's 1969 guidebook as summarised by Archnet. Other foreign consulates also operated in the city; Wikipedia's Karamanli page names only the US consulate, whose flagpole Yusuf Karamanli had cut down in May 1801. The old-city map from a travel site also lists an Old French Consulate.
today: Mapped in OpenStreetMap as "Old British Consulate"; its present use is not documented.
uncertain: The 1744 date and the house's use come from a single guidebook summary. Whether the OpenStreetMap point matches that exact house is unconfirmed. Locations of other consulates (US, French) were not found.

name: Gurgi Mosque
summary: A late Karamanli-era mosque near the harbour, built by a naval captain from Georgia and housing his family tomb.
history: Completed in 1834 for Mustafa Gurgi, a naval captain whose name means "from Georgia". It was built in the last years of Karamanli rule, after Pasha Yusuf Karamanli (reigned 1795-1832). It stands in the Bab al-Bahr district of the old city, near the sea, as part of a complex with a tomb and a school. The tomb of Gurgi and his family is in the antechamber. The Ottomans resumed direct control of Tripoli the following year, in 1835.
today: An active Sunni mosque and a tourist attraction. Coordinates are from the Wikipedia infobox.
uncertain: Nothing was found on its Gaddafi-era use or any restoration.

name: Tarabulus Military Storage Area Southeast (first confirmed Scud-B launcher)
summary: Where US imagery analysts first confirmed a Scud-B launcher in Libya, in April 1977, at a military storage area south-east of Tripoli.
history: A top-secret NPIC imagery information report of 21 April 1977 says the first confirmed Scud-B transporter-erector-launcher in Libya was identified at the 'Tarabulus Military Storage Area Southeast', at 32°49′45″N 13°20′26″E. It adds that four probable Scud-B launchers and nine resupply transporters had been seen in July 1976 at the Al Aziziyah ammunition storage depot.
era: 1976-1977; the later organisation of the Scud brigades is covered in the 1980 NPIC report.
today: Not described.
uncertain: Coordinates are exact in the report, but the report names the area only as a military storage area and does not say how long Scuds stayed there. Later Scud brigades were at other sites such as Bin Ghashir.
documented: Seen in US imagery in 1977; later use not documented

name: Ain Zara battlefield and memorial
summary: The oasis south-east of Tripoli where the Italians won the battle of 4 December 1911.
history: On 4 December 1911 about 12,000 Italians in three columns attacked about 8,000 Ottoman and Arab troops holding a well-fortified position with eight Krupp guns, about 8 km south of Tripoli. The Ottoman side withdrew in the afternoon and left its guns. Italian losses were 17 killed and 171 wounded, including Colonel Giovanni Pastorelli. The Italians then fortified the oasis and built a railway linking it to Tripoli. On 28 January 1912 about 4,000 Ottoman and Arab fighters tried to retake it and were repelled.
uncertain: The point is the OpenStreetMap "Memorial Ain Zara" node rather than the exact field. Casualty figures for the opposing forces are rough. Troops digging trenches found a Roman mosaic, probably from Oea, which was sent to Italy.

name: Mellaha Lake Grand Prix Circuit
summary: A fast 13 km road circuit around Mellaha Lake and airfield, home of the Tripoli Grand Prix.
history: The Grand Prix was held 14 times from 1925 to 1940, and from 1933 on the Mellaha Lake circuit, 13.14 km long, in a salt basin between Tripoli, Suq al Jum'ah and Tajura. A grandstand held up to 10,000, and a white concrete tower opposite it was the track's most distinctive feature. The race was tied to the state lottery, sold in 12-lire tickets from October 1932 with prizes of up to 3 million lire. The last race was on 12 May 1940, won by Giuseppe Farina. The airfield was built inside the circuit.
uncertain: A story of a fixed 1933 race is considered a probable myth. What remains of the grandstand and tower is not stated. Coordinates are Wikipedia's approximate circuit centre.

history: IAEA GOV/2004/12 Annex I: 'Site C: the original site for the Uranium Conversion Facility (Al Khalla)'. Paragraph 17: the conversion modules were stored around Tripoli until 1998, partly assembled at Sawani (Site G), then moved to Al Khalla; paragraph 18: later moved to Salah Eddin (Site D).
era: The conversion modules were later moved on to Salah Eddin. The site was cleared in 2004.
today: Not described in the pages seen.
uncertain: Suburb-level only. 'Khalla' is the name of a group of neighbourhoods in Salah al-Din (Khalla al-Ferjan, Khalla Bin Oun, with an 'Al Khalla Road' on OpenStreetMap); the sources do not say which one. Pinned at Khalla al-Ferjan with a 2.5 km radius.

name: El Ezeizia (Site K), construction-materials store

Annex II also lists an 'Al Ezeizia storage site' and an 'Al Ezeizia artillery refurbishment site' among places inspected for weapons capability. A 1980 CIA imagery report says Libya's first Scuds were seen in July 1976 at the 'Al Aziziyah Ammunition Storage Depot'.

today: Not described in the pages seen.

The Aziziyah match is now better supported: the Annex II entries (storage and artillery refurbishment) and the CIA's 'Al Aziziyah Ammunition Storage Depot' are both military stores at Al Aziziyah, and the CIA says SA-5 missiles at 'Al Azizyah' protected Rabta. The depot's exact position is still unpublished, so the pin stays on the town centre with a 3 km radius. Do not confuse it with Bab al-Aziziya in Tripoli.

In May 2011 construction was reported halted; the August battle and Saif's arrest ended the plan.

history: The Ottoman governor had it built between 1866 and 1870; Wikipedia's timeline gives 1870 and a photograph archive says "mid-19th century". It stands about 18 metres tall in Al-Sa'aa (Clock) Square, near the end of Souq al-Mushir, the Karamanli Mosque and the Red Castle. The square is also home to the brassware market.
today: Still a city landmark. The point shown is the mapped Clock Square (Meydan Assa'a) in OpenStreetMap, not the tower's own point.

name: US Embassy, Tripoli
summary: The US diplomatic mission in Libya, burned by a mob in December 1979 and closed until 2004.
era: The US had already withdrawn its ambassador in 1972. On 2 December 1979 protesters set fire to the embassy, angry over false claims of US involvement in the seizure of the Grand Mosque in Mecca. The US withdrew its remaining staff and closed the embassy. A US Interests Section returned on 8 February 2004 and became a Liaison Office on 24 June 2004.
today: In September 2011 an American flag was raised over the embassy compound in Tripoli.
uncertain: OpenStreetMap places the US embassy in the south of the city; the 1979 building may have been in a different place.

name: First Scud launch of the 2011 war (about 80 km east of Sirte)

era: NATO strikes reportedly destroyed the remaining Scuds, and by 2011 the Scud-B force was effectively ended.

The Hani area lies in the eastern oasis belt, about 1.5 km south-east of the coordinates Wikipedia gives for the Shar al-Shatt fighting of October 1911. The battle ran 23-26 October 1911; Ottoman and Arab forces attacked from the oasis and Italian reprisals followed.

name: Ministers and officers arrested over the December 1969 plot
text: The CIA reported that Defence Minister Adam al-Hawwaz and Interior Minister Musa Ahmad were arrested for plotting against the Revolutionary Command Council, and that about 100 army and police officers were arrested shortly afterwards. Where they were held is not stated. Moftah Sharef, a former air force officer, told the Tarikhi oral-history project that he was arrested two days after returning from Egypt in connection with the conspiracy led by Defence Minister Adam Hawwaz and Interior Minister Musa Ahmad, that 28 people were charged and he was the only one charged solely with withholding information, and that his sentence of one year was raised to 13 with no stated charge; he says he served the first 12 years in the ‘White Horse’ prison, later called the Black Horse. He does not give years.

name: Killings of army personnel around Tripoli
text: A CIA brief reported dissension in the army and some assassinations of army personnel in the Tripoli area, weeks after the coup. No names or places are given.

name: Engineer Mahmoud Bannoun dies under torture
text: An engineer arrested in early April 1980 in Tripoli died a few days later as a result of torture; his body was returned to his family in a sealed coffin. Where he was held is not stated.

name: Student Abdulaziz al-Gharabli dies in custody
text: A Tripoli student suspected of belonging to a political party died in January 1984 from torture and lack of medical care.

name: Abdullah al-Muslati executed in Tripoli Central Prison
text: A student arrested on 16 April 1973 and sentenced to prison was retried before the revolutionary courts, sentenced to death and executed in Tripoli Central Prison. The prison's location is not yet known for this map.

name: Hassan al-Kurdi executed in prison without trial
text: Arrested with hundreds of others in the spring of 1973 and accused with nine others of belonging to the Islamic Liberation Party, he was released by order of the Revolutionary Council in December 1973, re-arrested the same day, held without trial until 1977, sentenced to 15 years and then to life, and executed in prison without trial in April 1984.

name: Unrest at the Faculty of Engineering
text: Unrest at the Faculty of Engineering of the University of Tripoli led to arrests; one student detained then, Hafez al-Madani, was hanged on campus in 1984.

name: Arrests over the 1973 royalist plot
text: The government said it had crushed a plot led by a nephew of the deposed King Idris. Eleven men were arrested in Tripoli, including two former prime ministers, and Gaddafi said they would be tried without mercy. Where they were held is not stated.

name: Arrests after the August 1975 coup attempt
text: After the failed coup by Revolutionary Command Council members, the CIA reported that Bashir Hawadi was under arrest in Tripoli while Umar al-Muhayshi escaped to Tunisia. The place of detention is not named.

name: Iraqi embassy employee shot dead
text: Husayn Muhammad Ali, an Iraqi embassy employee, was shot three times outside the Iraqi embassy in Tripoli as he arrived for work and died in hospital. Libyan authorities arrested a young Palestinian Fatah member; the CIA says his real target was the Iraqi ambassador. The embassy's 1978 address is not known.

name: Food riots in Tripoli shops
text: A US magazine article kept in CIA files describes shoppers in one of Tripoli's large state supermarkets rioting over a shipment of bananas, and says two women were trampled to death in a similar riot about two months earlier. The shops are not named.

name: Libyan government claims of NATO strikes in Tripoli
text: Libyan state television said NATO strikes killed 19 civilians in Tripoli on 24 May 2011 and seven on 19 June, and fifteen at Sorman near Tripoli on 20 June. These are government claims reported by Wikipedia and were not independently confirmed here; no sites are given.

name: Revolutionary Guard Corps
text: Grew out of the Revolutionary Committees. It watched soldiers inside barracks, reportedly controlled ammunition at the main bases, and fought regular army units in Tripoli’s streets during a May 1985 coup attempt. No source gives its bases.

name: Police stations and checkpoints
text: No published source maps Tripoli’s police posts or checkpoints for this period.

name: Military intelligence prison, Tripoli
text: A former detainee describes being held there after the May 1984 arrests. Its location is not given. Abubaker Shareef says he was arrested at home on 13 May 1984, handcuffed and blindfolded with no accusation, warrant or lawyer, and held for about four months in cell no. 24 of the military intelligence prison until September 1984: ‘I knew I was there because I could hear the ships by the port.’ He says he was electrocuted, beaten and threatened with dogs, that the cells were damp and infested with insects and rats, and that he lost 20 kg; he was released with a warning that he would be kept under observation. His interview was recorded on 9 December 2012 at what the page calls the former military intelligence prison in Tripoli.

name: Tripoli Central Prison
text: An old prison, said to date from the Fascist period, where 21 people arrested in February 1982 were held without trial until 1984 and then moved to Abu Salim (Amnesty International, 1991; a 1980 JPRS translation of an exile appeal also names it). Arabic Wikipedia lists a student, Abdullah al-Maslati, as executed in the Central Prison in April 1984 after a retrial before the revolutionary courts. No source gives its address.

name: Tripoli military prison
text: Amnesty International names it as the place a prisoner of conscience was moved to in late 1980, with family visits allowed once every three months. No source gives its address.

name: Al-Ataba prison, Tripoli
text: Amnesty International says Sudanese and other African workers were held here in 1996. No source gives its address.

name: Tobacco-factory prison, Tripoli
text: Wikipedia says one of the most notorious hidden prisons of 2011 was set up in a tobacco factory in Tripoli, where inmates were reportedly given half a loaf of bread and a bottle of water a day. The Red Cross was denied access. No source gives its location.

name: Al-Ruwaimi prison
text: A Tripoli prison where 12 prisoners released by court order in June 2016 were found dead a day later (UNSMIL). It was among the sites the 444th Brigade took in May 2025. No source seen gives its coordinates or when it opened.

name: 7 April, the “Day of Judgement”
text: English Wikipedia says Gaddafi called the anniversary of the 7 April 1976 student protests the “Day of Judgement”. On 7 April 1977 students Omar Dabboub and Mohamed Ben Saoud were hanged in public in Benghazi after a military tribunal in Tripoli; the broadcast was shown on television. Some sources say executions were repeated every 7 April until the late 1980s; that is disputed and no Tripoli venue is named. The University of Tripoli, where students were attacked in 1976 and a student was hanged in April 1984, is on the map.

name: Firing-squad executions
text: Eighteen people were shot by firing squad: 14 in Tripoli and 4 in Benghazi, many of them foreign nationals. The Tripoli venue is not named. State media reported the numbers; Amnesty says a Libyan newspaper, Cerene, reported the 18 were convicted of premeditated murder and were from Chad, Egypt and Nigeria, and that the authorities had not named them. Amnesty said it feared the trials did not meet international fair-trial standards and that foreign nationals often lacked interpreters and consular access. Amnesty and the European Parliament condemned the executions.

name: Public executions
text: Public hangings were staged around 7 April anniversaries, including at universities and a sports arena. The documented cases with places are in Benghazi, outside this map, except the April 1984 hanging at the University of Tripoli.

name: Hanging of Muhammad ash-Shabani and other executions after the May 1984 raid
text: Tripoli radio announced that a Basic People's Congress, after reading his confession, ratified a death sentence and hanged Muhammad Sa'id ash-Shabani, described as a Muslim Brotherhood member recruited by American intelligence; the place name in the transcript is garbled. Survivors' accounts on tarikhi.org say eight men were executed in June 1984 in different towns, from Tobruk in the east to Nalut in the west, and that some hangings were shown live on television during Ramadan. No Tripoli location is given for this one.

name: Palestinian arrested in Tripoli over an alleged plot against Gaddafi
text: Libyan media said a Palestinian, named as Abd al-Qadir Musa al-Khatib, was arrested in Tripoli for planning to assassinate Gaddafi on behalf of the CIA. In his televised “confession” he said he had killed a guard at a Palestinian camp close to the command camp in Tripoli. This is the regime's account only; where he was held is not stated.

name: Reported attempt on Gaddafi and executions of officers
text: The Washington Post reported on 28 February 1982 that the CIA had concluded an attempt on Gaddafi's life was made in the last two weeks of December 1981, probably by army officers back from Chad, and that he may have been grazed by a bullet. Reports of the number of Libyans executed afterwards ranged from four to 640; US officials believed some had been. The place of the attack and of any executions is not given, and Libyan media denied a coup attempt on 10 January 1982.

name: Six officers executed on corruption charges
text: An exile commentary reprinted by the US JPRS service says six officers were executed by Gaddafi in July 1980 “allegedly in order to combat corruption” and claims they were really planning a revolt. Their names and where they were executed are not given, and the claim comes from a source hostile to the government.

name: French family arrested in Tripoli for “spying”
text: Denise Dupont, 58, and her sons Alain, 25, and Jean-Claude, 21, were arrested in Tripoli in April 1980, convicted of spying “for American imperialism and Zionism” and sentenced to life in prison on 20 February 1982. Gaddafi pardoned them in March 1982. Where they were held is not stated.

name: Iraqi-aligned Ba'th party members imprisoned or executed
text: A British trade magazine summarised in JPRS says the small but influential Iraqi-oriented Ba'th party in Tripoli had been “smashed” and many of its leaders imprisoned or executed. No names, dates or places are given.

name: British hostages arrested in Tripoli after the London embassy siege
text: After the shooting of a policewoman at the Libyan People's Bureau in London on 17 April 1984, Douglas Ledingham, head of the British Caledonian office in Tripoli, was arrested (FBIS says at Tripoli airport; Wikipedia says by soldiers on the evening of 17 April), and a businessman, John Campbell, was also held. Wikipedia says Ledingham and two other Britons were held at a building called the “Italian Mansion”, about 400 yards from the Italian embassy, and that four British hostages were freed after 294 days in February 1985. The embassy's position in 1984 is not given, so the place is not mapped.

name: Campaign of “physical liquidation” announced against opponents
text: Gaddafi told Libyans abroad to return by 11 June 1980 or be “liquidated”, and said in a Der Spiegel interview that the revolutionary committees could decide this without a trial. Exile groups link the campaign to the arrest and death in custody of people inside Libya, such as the lawyer Amir al-Daghis. A CIA paper of February 1982 says the main killing campaign ran from March to June 1981 before he ordered a pause. Most of the killings listed in these sources took place in Europe, not Tripoli.

name: Reported 4,000 detainees in detention camps
text: An exile report published in the JPRS “Libya: Human Rights Violations” series says about 4,000 people were held in detention camps simply for not applauding the regime, and that an April 1980 wave of killings began under the slogan of “fighting bribery”. These are unverified exile figures, with no camp names or places.

name: Naval officers reported executed after an alleged plot
text: An opposition article reprinted by JPRS lists four alleged attempts on Gaddafi's life and says that in the fourth, 21 Libyan naval officers were executed. No date, place or names are given, and it is not confirmed elsewhere in our files.

name: Arrests in Tripoli in May 1984 and a televised “confession”
text: Amnesty International's 1992 report says 'Abd al-Mun'im Qasem al-Najjar was arrested in Tripoli in May 1984, reportedly tortured at the time of his arrest, and that Libyan television broadcast his “confession”; it lists him among 1984 detainees believed to be held at Abu Salim. The place of arrest is not given more closely than Tripoli.

name: Arrest at Tripoli airport and later death sentence
text: Amnesty says 'Abd al-Hadi Shahin was arrested on arrival at Tripoli airport from Egypt in October 1982, was reportedly tortured during interrogation, was tried in 1987, sentenced to death and was held at Abu Salim. Where he was interrogated is not stated.

name: Aftermath of the 8 May 1984 attack: shootout, captures and searches
text: On 12 May 1984 security forces killed the man they named as the attack's leader in a shootout somewhere in Tripoli; on 14 May the news agency announced the capture of a 24-year-old said to belong to the Muslim Brotherhood, whose photo a Tripoli newspaper published; a week after the attack roadblocks and house searches continued and diplomats needed permission to travel to border areas and the south. No streets are named.

name: Two Italian engineers arrested on charges of plotting against Libya
text: Ali Akermi says Enzo Castelli and Edoardo Seliciato were arrested in August 1980 after Libyan agents were caught in European countries. Akermi shared a cell with Castelli, and both Italians were freed in October 1986 in an exchange. The prison is not named in the interview, so it is not mapped.

name: Gaddafi speech threatening opponents at Bab al-Azizia
text: Akermi says that in 1980 Gaddafi told an audience at Bab al-Azizia that he would “kill the men and capture the women and orphan the children” of oppositionists. This is a single recollection and I found no transcript, so it is kept as testimony only.

name: Shots fired into a football-match protest
text: Amnesty says a demonstration in Tripoli against giving a World Cup qualifier to Algeria ended when security forces fired into the crowd, killing at least one demonstrator; its fuller 1991 paper says a medical student, Taha Jalul, was allegedly killed. No street, stadium or square is named, so the place is not mapped.

name: Mass arrests in Tripoli and nearby towns after the January 1989 protests
text: Amnesty reports at least 211 people arrested in Tripoli and surrounding towns between January and April 1989, most of them apparently not involved in any violence; across Libya it counts at least 394 arrests from January 1989 to April 1990, one of whom is believed held at Abu Salim. Named cases include Dr 'Abdul-Naser al-Bashir Abu-Lseyen (arrested 19–20 January) and Fathi Mahmud 'Atiya al-'Abbar and Muhammad 'Ali Mamash, held without trial.

name: Televised hangings of six Islamists, February 1987 (Benghazi stadium)
text: Amnesty lists nine people executed in February 1987 for politically motivated offences. Fathi Terbil, in an interview with Tarikhi, says the executions were broadcast live: six civilians were hanged in a sports stadium he does not name, and three military men were shot by firing squad. The US State Department's report for 1987 also says six civilians were hanged in public and three soldiers shot, all televised, and that the group of nine was described as an “enemies of God” clique arrested in October 1986; it names no site. Jamestown's history of political Islam in Libya says the six were hanged in the sports stadium in Benghazi, after the arrest of nine alleged Muslim Brotherhood members in 1986 for the murder of a senior security official, so this was not in Tripoli; it is listed because it was shown to the whole country and Amnesty counts it among the 1987 executions.

name: Death sentences handed down by revolutionary courts, later commuted
text: Amnesty says Fathi al-Sha'iri and Mahmud al-Shaltat were reportedly sentenced to death in February 1985 after four years in detention; Hassan 'Ali Yahya Mu'ammar was summarily tried and sentenced in 1987; and in June 1988 the sentences of four soldiers, including these three and Usama al-Sanussi Shalluf, were commuted. All were believed held at Abu Salim.

name: Ahmad Tholthy arrested, April 1986
text: Ahmad Tholthy was arrested about twenty days after his family returned to Libya from London. His wife, Widad, told Tarikhi she heard nothing of him for a year. He was later held at Abu Salim; he says the intelligence chief Abdallah Senussi once asked him to take the blame for the Lockerbie bombing in return for release, which he refused. This is his own account. The place of arrest is not given.

name: Death of a prisoner of conscience, late 1988
text: Amnesty reports that 'Abd al-Qadir Muhammad Al Ya'qoubi, a prisoner of conscience, reportedly died in prison in late 1988. The prison is not named.

name: Gaddafi tells a Youth Camp to “cut his head”
text: Amnesty quotes Gaddafi telling members of a Youth Camp on 19 July 1990 that religious groups should be dealt with by cutting off the head of the person involved. The location is not stated, so the place is not mapped.

name: Reported coup attempts and mass executions of officers
text: The Washington Post reported on 12 April 1985, citing intelligence reports that US officials called reliable, that conservative officers tried a coup at a presidential villa outside Tripoli in early March 1985, that as many as 15 officers were executed, and that a second attempt on a convoy in early April led to the reported execution of at least 60 more. The paper says both were kept secret inside Libya, and I found no second source. The villa is not identified, so the place is not mapped. Wikipedia's history of Libya under Gaddafi separately says a coup attempt in May 1985 was blocked mainly by the Revolutionary Guard, which fought regular army units in a series of street battles; it names no place or casualties and the month differs from the Post's March and April, so these may be the same events or different ones.

name: Two men who took part in the 1984 hangings found killed
text: The same Washington Post report of 12 April 1985 says the public hanging of two Tripoli University students in 1984 had fuelled open dissent among the thousands of students made to watch, and that two people who took part in those executions were later found slain. No names or places are given and the claim is unconfirmed.

name: Two Tripoli arrests in January 1989: at a home and near a mosque
text: Amnesty says Ibrahim Saleh Marseet, a Tripoli Agricultural Bank employee, was seized by security forces at his Tripoli home, and that Muftah 'Ali Salem al-Gazwi was arrested at a mosque near his home in Tripoli. Both were held incommunicado and their whereabouts were unknown; neither address is given. 'Aqoub Yusuf Abu-Hatiya was arrested in Sabha by Revolutionary Committee members and taken to an unknown place in Tripoli.

name: Political science student arrested in Tripoli
text: Amnesty lists Tareq al-Sharef, a political science student, as arrested in Tripoli in September or October 1991 and believed held incommunicado. No place of arrest is given.

name: Chadian leader Goukouni Oueddei shot during his arrest
text: Wikipedia says Goukouni Oueddei, the exiled former Chadian president, was placed under house arrest in Tripoli in August 1985 after Libya disapproved of his plans to negotiate with Hissène Habré, and that in October 1985 Libyan police arrested him and shot him in the stomach. He later left for Algiers in February 1987. The address is not given.

name: Alleged arrest of a Tunisian with a suitcase bomb
text: Wikipedia's article on the National Front for the Salvation of Libya says Libyan intelligence later claimed it had stopped an NFSL bombing campaign in 1987 and that a Tunisian was arrested in Tripoli carrying a suitcase bomb. This is a claim made by Libyan intelligence, with no place or name given.

name: Gaddafi on the prisoners freed in 1988
text: In a television interview broadcast on 3 May 1988 (FBIS), Gaddafi said men sentenced after the two earlier attempts on the revolution had faced execution or life terms “without investigation”, that he had delayed the beheading of those who tried to “steal the revolution”, and that at times of transformation many innocent people are sacrificed. On 12 June 1988, speaking at a hall he called Freedom Hall, he presented the Green Document, saying the death penalty would apply only to someone whose life endangers society. The hall's location is not stated in the translation.

name: Six men executed after a television announcement
text: Libyan television announced on 10 November 1992 that six men had been sentenced to death and executed that morning for offences including rape and murder, and showed pictures of them before execution the next day. Amnesty did not know their names and, citing the code of criminal procedure, says executions generally take place in prisons without naming the prison. These were the first officially announced executions in more than five years, according to Amnesty's 1993 paper. No place is given, so this is not mapped.

name: Foreign special forces and CIA help for the 2011 rebels (reported)
text: Reuters reported on 31 March 2011, citing government sources, that President Obama had signed a secret “finding” authorising covert US support for the rebels; the White House said no decision had been made on arming them. The New York Times, as quoted by the Atlantic Council, said CIA officers were in Libya, including former staff of the Tripoli station, and that dozens of British special forces and MI6 officers were reportedly operating there, with US officials saying the Western operatives were not directing the rebels. A Washington Post report dated 22 August 2011 says British, French and Qatari special forces were on the ground advising the rebels, that the US shared satellite and drone imagery and intercepts, and that CIA operatives inside Libya contributed; it describes the plan as a pincer from the south and west. Wikipedia's article on the battle adds that British and Qatari authorities supplied communications equipment to rebel cells in Tripoli, and one Russian-language report says Qatari special forces took part in the assault on the compound, which I could not confirm. None of these sources names a Tripoli address.

name: Tripoli militia clashes, October 2017
text: Wikipedia's list of western Libya clashes gives several: on 1 October the Tripoli Revolutionaries Brigade fought the Nawasi Brigade in Gurji (Massara) and near the Brigade's headquarters in Shara al-Shatt, leaving three dead; on 4 October the Brigade and others took camps at Qasr Bin Ghashir, Sayah and Wadi Rabea from Gaddafi loyalists, with two killed; on 6 October two brigades fought in Arada and Ain Zara, leaving four dead and 17 injured; and on 16–17 October Rada fought armed youths in Ghararat near Mitiga airport and the Nawasi Brigade fought Brigade 50 at the port. I read these only in Wikipedia's table and did not open the original reports.

name: Bashagha's government enters Tripoli and fighting follows
text: Wikipedia says the parliament-appointed government of Fathi Bashagha arrived in Tripoli on 17 May 2022, that this led to several hours of fighting between armed groups, and that the government team had to withdraw. The article names no neighbourhoods or casualties for this day.

name: Heavy fighting across Tripoli, 26–27 August 2022
text: The unity government's health ministry reported 32 killed and 159 injured. Libya Security Monitor says the fighting began between Haithem Tajouri's 777 Brigade and groups tied to the Internal Security Agency and spread through more than a dozen armed groups, with pro-Bashagha forces trying to use it to remove Prime Minister Dbeibah and failing. NBC reported an earlier toll of 23 dead, including the comedian Mustafa Baraka, with 64 families evacuated, hospitals shelled and ambulances barred from reaching civilians, and the UN mission describing indiscriminate medium and heavy shelling of civilian neighbourhoods. The International Rescue Committee described the dead as civilians. None of these sources names the districts hit, so it is not mapped.

name: Coup seizures in Tripoli, 1 September 1969
text: Wikipedia says the Free Officers' coup was launched at Benghazi and finished within two hours, and that military control of Tripoli was established within a few days. In Tripoli, Umar Muhayshi took over the Tripoli barracks, Abdessalam Jalloud seized the city's anti-aircraft batteries, and Khweldi Hameidi took the Tripoli radio station and was sent to arrest Crown Prince Hasan ar-Rida. Airports, police depots, radio stations and government offices in Tripoli and Benghazi were occupied. The article names no street or address and gives no casualty figures, so it is not mapped.

name: Mutiny reported against orders to invade Tunisia, 31 August 1985
text: An FBIS report of 3 September 1985, citing Egypt's Al-Ahram via the Middle East News Agency, says army and air force units mutinied on 31 August, refusing orders to invade Tunisia; that Gaddafi's special forces put it down and arrested 43 senior officers; and that the air force mutineer, a base commander near the Tunisian border, tried to send aircraft against Gaddafi's headquarters. It adds that Libyan media had not reported any rebellion. A Washington Post column of 6 November 1985 says the loyal guards, including East Germans, halted the planes and tanks the mutineers had ordered to attack Tripoli, and that at least 13 senior air force officers and 30 army officers were arrested. The two accounts differ on the numbers, and both rest on unnamed sources. The headquarters is not named, so this is not mapped.

name: Battalion mutiny at Tarhuna after the US raid, 16 April 1986
text: A CIA talking-points memo from May 1986 says a battalion of troops apparently mutinied at Tarhuna, outside Tripoli, on 16 April and was put down by loyal air force units, and that there were also skirmishes between regular troops and the Revolutionary Committees in the immediate aftermath of the raids. Tarhuna is a town some 60 km from the city, so it is not mapped; the gun battle seen at Bab al-Aziziya in the same days is on the map.

name: First aerial reconnaissance and first bombing, October–November 1911
text: The Italo-Turkish War article says the first aerial reconnaissance flight took place on 23 October 1911 and the first aerial bombing on 1 November 1911 near Tajura and Ain Zara. The Shar al-Shatt article names the 23 October pilots as Captain Carlo Maria Piazza and Captain Riccardo Moizo, and adds that their flights were not real reconnaissance. The exact spots bombed are not given.

name: Attacks on fuel stations in Tripoli, claimed for September 1979
text: A Cairo magazine, Akhir Sa'a, quoted by the Middle East News Agency and translated by JPRS in December 1979, said opposition forces made a surprise attack on six fuel stations in Tripoli and one in Zuwarah on a night in September, and that the plan was made in Tripoli, Zuwarah and Sabha. The same report claims a bombing at Surt that killed 80 people. It is an Egyptian press claim during a hostile period, the date is garbled in the translation, and I found no second source, so treat it as unconfirmed. The stations are not named.

name: Eight men executed after a military trial, announced 2 January 1997
text: Amnesty says eight men were executed on 2 January 1997: Colonel Miftah Qarrum al-Wirfalli, Major Ramadhan al-'Ayhuri, Major Khalil Salam Mohammad al-Jidiq, Colonel Mostafa Abu al-Qassim Mas'ud al-Kikli, Lieutenant-Colonel Sa'ad Saleh Farag, Major Mostafa Ihbayl al-Firjani, Dr Sa'ad Misbah al-'Amin al-Zubaydi and Sulayman Ghayth Miftah, six of them senior officers and two civilians. Libyan television said the Supreme Military Court had upheld the sentences for passing defence secrets to a foreign state (the United States) and belonging to the banned National Front for the Salvation of Libya. Six other officers and two civilians were acquitted. Amnesty says three of the eight had appeared on television in March 1994 confessing to spying for the US and were allegedly tortured into confessing; they had been arrested after the October 1993 rebellion by army units around Misrata. Executed Today adds that the National Front said the real offence was the failed 1993 revolt. Neither source names the court, the prison or the place of execution, so it is not mapped.

name: People's Court in Tripoli sentences two to death in the Islamic Group trial
text: Amnesty says 152 professionals and students arrested in 1998 on suspicion of backing the banned Libyan Islamic Group, which it says was not known to have used or advocated violence, were held in secret detention for over two years, and that on 16 February 2002 a People's Court in Tripoli sentenced Abdullah Ahmed Izzedin and Salem Abu Hanak to death. Amnesty reports 73 others got life, 11 got ten years and 66 were acquitted. Some defendants alleged torture and no thorough investigation is known. The appeal opened in summer 2002 and was repeatedly adjourned; Amnesty believed the 86 men still held were at Abu Salim. A Jamestown article reports an appeal court upheld the two death sentences and the ten-year terms on 2 December, with the year not stated clearly in the page I read. The State Department says the government released 86 Muslim Brotherhood prisoners from Abu Salim on 2 March 2006, which matches the number Amnesty said were still held. The court building is not named. Amnesty’s urgent action of 20 February 2002 adds that the hearings were closed and held in a military compound in the suburbs of Tripoli, that the trial opened in March 2001, that at the second session on 29 April 2001 lawyers chosen by the families were refused entry and the judge appointed clerks from the Popular Lawyers’ Office instead, and that Amnesty applied twice to observe the trial and was refused. The US State Department’s report for 2005 says Amnesty raised concerns about 86 Muslim Brotherhood prisoners at Abu Salim who held a seven-day hunger strike over delays in their appeal (reported in connection with Amnesty’s February 2004 visit) and that on 9 October the Supreme Court ordered a retrial of 86 activists sentenced in 2002, with no new trial begun by the end of the year.

name: Trial of the Bulgarian nurses and Palestinian doctor in Tripoli
text: RFE/RL's timeline says five Bulgarian nurses, a Bulgarian doctor, a Palestinian doctor and nine Libyans went on trial in Tripoli in February 2000 on charges of deliberately infecting hundreds of children with HIV, with the trial postponed repeatedly amid allegations of torture. The medics were sentenced to death in May 2004; the Supreme Court overturned the verdicts on 25 December 2005 and ordered a retrial, which began on 11 May 2006; a court sentenced the six to death again in December 2006 and the Supreme Court upheld the sentences on 11 July 2007. Amnesty says a Tripoli court acquitted police officers and a doctor of torturing them in June 2005, and describes electric shocks, beatings and suspension by the arms. The hospital involved, al-Fateh Children's Hospital, is in Benghazi, and neither source names the Tripoli court building or the prison.

name: Dissident Fathi al-Jahmi held in Tripoli, 2002–2009
text: Human Rights Watch says internal security forces arrested Fathi al-Jahmi on 19 October 2002 after he criticised Gaddafi, a court sentenced him to five years, an appeals court ordered his release in March 2004, and agents arrested him again on 26 March 2004 with his wife and eldest son. A secret trial began in late 2005 and in May 2006 a court found him mentally unfit and sent him to a psychiatric hospital; in July 2007 he was moved to the Tripoli Medical Center, where Human Rights Watch and Physicians for Human Rights visited him in March 2008 and found state security officers controlling access. Amnesty's report for 2009 says he was released from jail in a coma in May 2009. A medical journal article says he was flown to Jordan on 5 May 2009 and died there on 20 May 2009, aged 68. Amnesty's 2004 report puts him at Ain Zara at one point (see the Ain Zara prison pin). The location of his first detention is not given.

name: Ismail al-Khazmi dies in custody in a Tripoli prison
text: The US State Department's 2010 country report says Ismail al-Khazmi was taken from his workplace, reportedly tortured in a Tripoli prison and died in custody, and that the government held no transparent inquiry into the death. It does not name the prison or give the exact date.

name: Arrests before a planned Tripoli demonstration, and sentences for eleven men
text: The World Organisation Against Torture says eleven men were arrested on 16 and 17 February 2007 over a planned peaceful demonstration in Tripoli against the authorities, to mark the first anniversary of a Benghazi demonstration in which at least 12 people were killed. On 10 June 2008 a state security court in Tripoli, reportedly inside Abu Salim prison, sentenced them to between six and 25 years: writer Jamal al-Hajji, Dr Idris Bufayed, writer Fareed Azway, lawyer Almahdi Hmeed and Assadiq, Faraj and Ali Hmeed, Ala Adrisi, Assadiq Gashoot, Bashir Alharis and Ahmad Alabeedi; Adel Hmeed was reportedly released the same day. Before trial some were held at Jdeida or Ain Zara. Dr Bufayed was treated for cancer at a hospital in Sabratha. The State Department's report for 2006 adds that Idrees Mohammed Boufayed (the same man, spelled differently) was ordered to report to the Internal Security Agency's main office in Tripoli after returning from Switzerland on 30 September 2006, was detained on 5 November and released on 29 December. Amnesty says al-Hajji was released in March 2009 and arrested again on 9 December 2009 (see the Jdeida prison pin). The planned demonstration site is not named, so this is not mapped.

name: Migrants pushed back by Italy to Tripoli, May–July 2009
text: Human Rights Watch says that on 6 May 2009 an Italian patrol boat intercepted about 80 migrants whose boat had drifted for at least 48 hours and landed them at a dock in Tripoli, where Libyan authorities immediately detained them; that on 18 June 2009 about 75 migrants were handed to a Libyan patrol boat, taken to Tripoli and handed to a Libyan military unit; and that on 1 July 2009 UNHCR interviewed 82 people, 76 of them Eritreans, returned by the Italian navy, who said they were given no food during a 12-hour operation, had their papers confiscated and were all detained on arrival. Migrants told Human Rights Watch that police and thugs entered their homes in Tripoli and Benghazi to attack, extort and arrest them, and that smugglers held some as virtual prisoners in those cities. Libya did not let Human Rights Watch visit migrant detention centres in April 2009. The dock and the detention sites in Tripoli are not named.

name: Opponents returned to Libya by the US and UK, 2004
text: Human Rights Watch says Abdul Hakim Belhadj, seized in Malaysia with British help and held briefly by the CIA in Thailand, was sent to Libya around 9 March 2004 and received by Musa Kusa; that Sami al-Saadi was rendered from Hong Kong days after Tony Blair's visit of 25 March 2004; and that Khalid al-Sharif, after about two years in US custody, was abused again in Libya and sentenced to death by firing squad. All three were released on 23 March 2010. Mohammed Shoroeiya, Saleh Di'iki and Majid al-Maghrebi were returned around 22 August 2004; Shoroeiya was sentenced to life and released on 16 February 2011. The visible part of the report does not say where in Libya they were held, so none of this is mapped.

name: Police sweeps against migrants in Tripoli, 2002–2005
text: Human Rights Watch says police ran sweeps in the Tajura market on Tuesdays and Thursdays in 2002, where a Darfur man was held five days with more than 100 people and then about two months without charge; that in mid-2004 street sweeps and house-to-house raids in Tripoli sent detainees to a facility a Liberian witness called “Janzur”, a small open building without food or healthcare, where he claimed some died of suffocation, trauma and hunger; that in September 2004 police arrested 31 refugees and asylum seekers holding UNHCR letters, most held at the al-Fellah deportation facility until African Union ambassadors intervened; that in October 2004 the government prepared to deport hundreds after Italy returned migrants and refused UNHCR access; and that in April–May 2005 Human Rights Watch visited al-Fellah and interviewed nine people awaiting deportation. The report says the earlier violence in Zawiya in September 2000 killed up to fifty according to press reports and seven according to the government. The al-Fellah and Janzur sites are not located, and the Gurji raid of September 2003 is on the map.

name: Two Swiss businessmen barred from leaving Libya, 2008–2010
text: Swissinfo says Max Göldi and Rachid Hamdani were arrested in July 2008 and prevented from leaving Libya after the arrest of one of Muammar Gaddafi's sons in Geneva; on 30 November 2009 Göldi was sentenced to 16 months and fined for visa violations, which was cut on appeal to four months plus a fine for illegally doing business. Hamdani was acquitted on appeal, got an exit visa on 22 February 2010 and returned to Switzerland. Göldi gave himself up in February 2010 and was taken to prison in handcuffs in Tripoli; his lawyer said he was released on 10 June 2010. The article does not name the prison, and the earlier detention was in effect a travel ban.

name: Deportation of Libyans from Tripoli to Italian islands
text: Francesca Di Pasquale writes that on 24 October 1911 Prime Minister Giolitti telegraphed General Caneva in Tripoli ordering the immediate deportation to Italy of all ‘arrested rioters’; the arrests were made en masse and took in beggars, labourers, peasants, wealthy owners and storekeepers, and old men, women and minors were sent too. Most of those deported from Tripoli went to Ustica and Tremiti, and the first arrived on Ustica aboard the steamship Rumania on 29 October 1911. She says 127 of 900 Libyans sent to Ustica died (about 17%) and 437 of 1,366 sent to Tremiti (about a third), and gives total deportations to Italy over the colonial period as about 4,000 (Mario Missori, 1911–1918) to 5,000–6,000 (Libyan Studies Centre). A 2025 article by Galadriel Ravelli says Ustica alone received more than 2,000 deportees from Libya over two decades and has the only Italian cemetery given over to Libyan deportees. Neither source names the embarkation port or a detention site in Tripoli, so this is not mapped.

name: Allied bombing of the Jewish Quarter, winter 1942–43
text: Wikipedia’s article on the Buq Buq labour camp says the freed prisoners who reached Tripoli in mid-November 1942 found their community in chaos, with the Jewish Quarter ‘frequently bombed by Allied forces’ as the Axis retreated through it. The article gives no dates, targets or casualties. This sits oddly with an Australian War Memorial photo caption of 26 January 1943, which says few bombs fell in the residential quarter and the harbour took the brunt, so the claim is reported here as a single-source statement. The wider air campaign is on the port marker.

name: Buq Buq forced-labour camp for Libyan Jewish men
text: Wikipedia says Italy ran a forced-labour camp at Buq Buq, on the Egyptian side of the border, from August to November 1942 for 350 Libyan Jewish men aged 18 to 45, mostly from Tripoli and the surrounding area. The sick and injured were sent back to Tripoli after an Italian army doctor examined them, which cut the numbers to just over 200 by the end of October; the RAF bombed the camp in late October, Italy dissolved it on 6 November 1942 after El Alamein, and the prisoners had to walk back across the desert, reaching Tripoli in mid-November. In 2002 Germany accepted responsibility for the imprisonment of Jews in six Libyan camps, including Buq Buq. The camp was in Egypt, so it is not mapped.

name: Italian race laws against Tripoli’s Jews
text: Wikipedia says that in the late 1930s the Fascist regime in Italian Libya began passing antisemitic laws: Jews were dismissed from government jobs and some from government schools, and their citizenship papers were stamped ‘Jewish race’. The governor, Italo Balbo, partly opposed them. In 1941 about a quarter of Tripoli’s population was still Jewish, with 44 synagogues in the city.

name: Trials and compensation after the 1945 riots
text: Wikipedia says at least 550 Libyans were arrested and tried by British military courts. Sources disagree on what followed: a Jewish Refugees article says only 289 of the roughly 550 were tried, most were freed months later and the British arrested ten Jews for defending themselves; Lyn Julius, in an opinion piece, says only 34 were tried and 25 got five-year sentences. The same article gives the official damage figure as 268 million Military Administration lire, says the Jewish community assessed it as much higher, and says the British avoided paying the reparations the community demanded.

name: Small riots and bombs against Italian interests in Tripoli
text: A CIA intelligence summary for the week ending 22 September 1948 says fear of a return of Italian rule led to a number of small-scale riots in the city of Tripoli, where anti-Italian feeling was especially high. It says a bomb was placed outside the office of the Italian airline and another bomb damaged the home of a pro-Italian Arab, and that the announcement of US–UK proposals for separate treatment of Cyrenaica and Tripolitania also angered Tripolitanian nationalists, who mostly favoured a united independent Libya. The summary says no rioting followed that announcement. It gives no street addresses or casualties.

name: Bomb attempt on Emir Idris and a hostile reception in Tripolitania
text: A CIA bulletin of 27 May 1951, citing the US Consul General in Tripoli, says the Emir’s tour of Libya ran into political trouble after a recent bombing attempt on his life and a generally hostile reception in Tripolitania, and warns that abandoning the tour would hurt the UN plan for an independent Libya. A June 1952 CIA estimate says he was ‘greeted with a bomb’ on his last visit to Tripolitania in 1951. An April 1951 bulletin reports an ‘unhealthy’ political situation in Tripoli, with Bashir Saadawi making inflammatory speeches against the US over land for Wheelus. None of the documents says where the bomb was thrown.

name: Election disorders in Tripolitania, February 1952
text: A CIA estimate of June 1952 says the government deported National Congress Party leader Bashir Saadawi shortly after the 19 February elections because his party was responsible for disorders ‘bordering on revolt’, which it says killed 8 people and left 110 other casualties. Wikipedia’s election article reports one person killed and a British police officer injured at Misrata, tear gas used, three Tripolitanian constituencies delayed to March after rioters destroyed the electoral register, and all parties banned afterwards; a University of Central Arkansas dataset likewise lists one death. The sources do not say how many of the casualties were in Tripoli itself.

name: Pro-Egyptian demonstration in Tripoli
text: A CIA bulletin of 12 September 1956 says the Libyan police kept control during pro-Egyptian demonstrations in Benghazi on 9 August and in Tripoli on 16 August 1956, and reports a claim that Egypt was preparing sabotage of British installations in Libya. The CIA comment says no ‘nationalist units’ were known to exist in Libya, though the reference might be to the banned National Congress Party. No place in Tripoli is named.

name: Crowds outside the Egyptian and Soviet embassies
text: A CIA bulletin of 27 October 1956 says that after the French capture of five Algerian FLN leaders on 22 October, anti-French demonstrations occurred in Amman and in Tripoli, ‘where crowds demonstrated enthusiastically outside the Egyptian and Soviet embassies’. It gives no addresses, numbers or casualties.

name: Pro-Nasser demonstrations during King Saud’s visit
text: A CIA estimate of 7 May 1957 says ‘well-organized pro-Nasser demonstrations were staged in Tripoli’ during the recent visit of King Saud of Saudi Arabia, and that Nasser’s picture was displayed in Libyan cities and towns. It gives no dates, places or casualties.

name: Rioting in Tripoli by pro-Nasser students
text: A CIA bulletin of 21 March 1959 says ‘violent and large-scale rioting’ took place in Tripoli on 20 March, sparked by well-organized students demonstrating in favour of Nasser and against Qasim and the Communists, and was the third and most violent of a series of pro-Nasser demonstrations in Libya that week. The CIA judged it unrelated to US–Libyan relations, which were then at a point where Libya was proposing new terms for the Wheelus base. The bulletin gives no place in Tripoli, casualties or arrests.

name: Attacks on US offices and the evacuation of Americans
text: US State Department files say Libya’s Foreign Ministry warned on 1 June 1967 that flights from Wheelus could be read as supplying Israel, and that ‘angry demonstrations and attacks against U.S. offices in Libya’ followed the start of the war on 5 June. A telegram of 13 June says about 6,300 Americans had been evacuated from Libya by 11 June, 3,305 civilians remained (530 of them employees and dependents at Wheelus) and 3,346 US military personnel were still on the base; it describes the security situation in the Tripoli area as improving, and a later footnote says Libyan security officials had the situation under control by 15 June. The documents report no casualties and name no particular building. The attacks on Jewish homes are on the 1967 riots marker.

name: Habib Bourguiba arrested in Libya and deported
text: A CIA report of 7 September 1948 says the Tunisian Neo-Destour leader Habib Bourguiba entered Libya illegally to make Tripoli his advance base for directing Tunisian nationalist activity, was apprehended by the British authorities and was deported to Egypt on 7 May. It adds that the British administration had heard that Bourguiba’s assistant, Salih ben Yusuf, was on his way from Cairo to Tripoli for the same purpose. The report does not say where in Libya he was arrested or held.

name: Internment order for the Jews of Tripolitania and Cyrenaica
text: Wikipedia says that on 7 February 1942 Mussolini ordered the internment of the Jews of Cyrenaica and Tripolitania, to move them from the war zone and stop them aligning with the British. Of Tripolitanian Jews, only those with British or French citizenship were sent to the Giado camp in the Nafusa mountains, about 153 km south-west of Tripoli; those with Libyan citizenship were sent to labour camps such as Buq Buq and Sidi Azaz. Sick prisoners were at first sent back to Tripoli, prisoners accused of serious crimes went to a criminal prison in Tripoli, and the Tripoli Jewish community sent food and information to the camp. After the British liberated Giado in January 1943 the surviving prisoners were brought to Tripoli for housing and medical care. Giado is outside Tripoli, so it is not mapped.

name: Eleven officers reportedly hanged after a plot to blow up Gaddafi’s car
text: The Cairo weekly Akhir Sa’ah, citing diplomatic sources in Tripoli, said Libyan intelligence had arrested pilots who were about to bomb Gaddafi’s headquarters and had hanged 11 officers accused of placing explosives in his car, without trial, including the officer who exposed the plan. It said Gaddafi watched the hangings and had armed loyal tribes from Sirte for protection. The report was relayed by the Cairo news agency and reprinted in a JPRS digest. It names no one, gives no place or exact date, and no second source was found, so it is treated as unconfirmed.

name: Army officers shot by firing squad after the 1975 plot
text: Amnesty International’s May 1977 newsletter says a group of army officers convicted of plotting to overthrow the government in August 1975 was executed on 2 April 1977 and that ‘the exact numbers involved are not known’. It says a military court tried a group of 75 people in December 1976 and condemned 23 to death, one in absentia, and that a second military court raised the death sentences to 45 on appeal. It adds that official Libyan sources said five civilians were hanged in public in Benghazi on 7 April for ‘terrorist sabotage’. The counts differ: a statement by a group calling itself the Libyan Citizens Grouping, printed in Cairo on 14 April 1980 and translated by JPRS, says 21 officers aged 21 to 27 were shot on 2 April 1977, and that three students were driven from Tripoli Central Prison at 5 a.m. on 7 April to Benghazi, 1,000 km away, and hanged in the square in front of the Socialist Union building from 3 p.m. to 8 p.m.; Wikipedia names two students, Omar Dabboub and Mohamed Ben Saoud. A second exile publication in JPRS says in general terms that students, officers and ordinary citizens were shot or hanged that April. No source names a place for the firing squad, so nothing is mapped. The Benghazi hangings are on the unplaced list under the 7 April entry.

name: Alleged torture deaths and ‘car accident’ killings of officers, 1970s
text: The same Libyan Citizens Grouping statement claims that Colonel al-Majiri and Captain al-Barghuthi died under torture during the purges it describes, and that Revolution Council member Captain Muhammad al-Maqrif, an officer called al-Harathi, Captain ‘Atiyah al-Kasih and the civilian Miftah al-Hindbany were each killed and their deaths put down to car accidents. It says an investigating committee under al-Maqrif was formed and its findings buried, and that mothers, wives and children queued outside Tripoli Central Prison to visit the arrested and condemned. None of this is confirmed by another source here; the statement is a one-sided appeal and gives no dates for the deaths.

name: Dawn raids and annual ‘April round-ups’, 1978–1980 (exile account)
text: The Libyan Citizens Grouping says that from February 1978 a group of contractors, teachers, businessmen, students and officers were taken by military intelligence and tortured for about six months amid rumours they would be executed the next April, and that on 10 February 1980 revolutionary committees raided homes at dawn, accusing people of taking commissions from foreign firms or of sending money abroad. It describes masked men in green tunics collecting people from their doorsteps from lists, and interrogation by beating the soles of the feet and electric shock. It also says a Benghazi contractor, Tawfiq Bin-Sa’ud, died in a bomb blast in April 1979 and that many people were then arrested because his name list was said to include theirs; that part belongs to Benghazi. The Cairo paper printed it as an opposition appeal and none of it is independently confirmed.

name: Cultural Revolution purges of students and officers
text: English Wikipedia says Gaddafi announced a cultural revolution in a speech at Zuwara on 15 April 1973 and that the purges of 1973 first concentrated on university students in Tripoli and Benghazi and on army officers. The Libyan Citizens Grouping statement describes the same speech but dates it to February 1974, says lists of ‘the educated and nationalist youth’ had been prepared hours before it, that homes were raided and books, Marxist and Islamic alike, were burned, and that the five points of the speech were posted on a placard in front of the Ministry of Justice on Omar al-Mukhtar Street in Tripoli. The two sources differ by almost a year on the date; Wikipedia’s is the better documented. Arrests that spring are on the unplaced list under the 1973 student cases.

name: Expulsion of the Italians and the ‘Day of Revenge’
text: Wikipedia says the Revolutionary Command Council issued a law on 21 July 1970 to ‘regain wealth stolen from the Libyan people by Italian oppressors’, that Italians who had long lived in Libya had to leave by 7 October 1970, that about 20,000 were expelled with their property confiscated, and that 7 October became a national holiday, the Day of Revenge, which was cancelled in 2004, brought back the next year and later renamed the Day of Friendship. Wikipedia says Italians made up 37 percent of Tripoli’s population in 1939, and its article on Italian refugees says 24,000 of the 27,000 Italians still in Libya in 1964 lived in the Tripoli area. No Tripoli street, cemetery or building is named in these sources, so nothing is mapped.

name: Libya’s last Jews: arrests, confiscation and departure
text: Wikipedia’s history of the Jews in Libya says that after the 1967 exodus about 200 Jews remained when Gaddafi took power, that under his rule all Jewish men were arrested and taken to police stations, all Jewish property was confiscated and all debts to Jews were cancelled, that emigration was banned but most of the rest left, and that fewer than 40 Jews remained by 1972. The same article says the 1970 ‘Day of Expulsion’ celebrated the expulsion of British and Italians, while the article on the Day of Revenge says some sources claim it also marked the expulsion of Libyan Jews; the sources do not agree on this. The arrests and confiscations are given without dates, places or numbers, so nothing is mapped. The pogroms of 1945, 1948 and 1967 are on the map.

name: Foiled plan to land mercenaries and free 150 prisoners from the Tripoli prison
when: January – April 1971 (CIA); ‘mid-1970’ in a later book review
text: A CIA status report of May 1971, published by the State Department, says the agency uncovered a plan for a maritime operation to land a small European mercenary force in Libya to release 150 political prisoners from ‘the Tripoli prison’, men who had held office under the former regime and who would then disperse into the countryside as the core of an anti-regime force. It says two attempts were made, in late January or early February and in late March or early April 1971; that the second involved about 25 foreign mercenaries and two vessels, one held in Trieste and one detained by Moroccan authorities in Casablanca; that the plot was backed by the old-regime politician Umar al-Shalhi; and that it had no real chance of overthrowing the regime. A December 1982 book review of John Cooley’s Libyan Sandstorm, held in the CIA reading room, tells a version of the same plot, code-named ‘the Hilton assignment’, in which mercenaries would land on the coast near Tripoli, free political prisoners from ‘Libya’s main prison’, arm them and attack Gaddafi’s residence in the nearby barracks; it dates it to mid-1970 and says Western police stopped it at least three times. The two accounts differ on the date and on what the prisoners would do; the CIA report is the contemporary one. Neither names the prison, so nothing is mapped. The same CIA report counts at least seven counter-coup attempts inside Libya in the first sixteen months after the revolution, plus one from Chad.

name: Gaddafi limits revolutionary-committee death sentences
text: Speaking live from Ra’s Lanuf on the tenth anniversary of the US bases’ departure, Gaddafi asked the revolutionary committees to stop their operations around the world and not to carry out death sentences except on people convicted by a revolutionary court, with an exception for anyone shown to have dealt with Egyptian, Israeli or US authorities, who he said deserved death anywhere. He said hundreds of Libyans who had fled had returned after his ultimatum. The speech followed the campaign announced in February 1980 and the London embassy dispute, and does not say whether any killings inside Tripoli stopped.

name: Muslim Brotherhood member executed in Tripoli
text: The Library of Congress country study says the Muslim Brotherhood was banned in Libya in the mid-1980s but was present, that a member was executed in Tripoli in 1983, and that a group of adherents was arrested in 1986 after the murder of a high-ranking political official in Benghazi. It names no one and gives no place of execution or date within 1983. The 7 April 1983 hanging of the student Mohammed Haffaf is on the map and may be a different case.

name: Omar al-Muhayshi reportedly beaten to death at Tripoli airport
when: Reported 13 November 1985; handover said to follow the 1984 Morocco–Libya treaty
text: A syndicated Jack Anderson and Dale Van Atta column in the Washington Post says that Omar al-Muhayshi, a former member of the Revolutionary Command Council who fled to Tunisia after the aborted August 1975 plot and later found refuge in Morocco, was handed over by King Hassan to Gaddafi as part of the deal for ending Libyan aid to the Polisario, and was ‘beaten and kicked to death’ by Gaddafi’s men on the airport runway in Tripoli. The column cites unnamed US intelligence sources, does not say which airport or give a date, and admits it is not clear whether Gaddafi’s agents kidnapped him or Morocco put him on the plane. It also says most of his co-plotters were rounded up and executed the following March. Amnesty’s 1991 report gives a shorter and slightly different account: it says ‘Umar al-Mahishi, a former Revolution Command Council member who reportedly led an abortive coup in 1975 and escaped, was forcibly returned from Morocco together with Nuri al-Falah, was detained from 1984, and ‘was apparently executed on arrival’, with no date or place given. The two sources agree on the handover and the death but not on how or exactly when he died.

name: Gaddafi frees prisoners and orders a Tripoli prison pulled down
text: FBIS carried a live Tripoli television speech of 3 March 1988 in which Gaddafi told a group of prisoners at ‘Tripoli Prison’ that they would be freed within minutes and that ‘this terrible wall will be demolished’. He said some of those freed had been sentenced to death and that the charge against them was ‘lack of knowledge’, not treason. A Libyan statement carried in the same FBIS issue said 400 inmates were freed after the leader demolished the prison where they were held, and the foreign liaison bureau told embassies to arrange the release of foreign prisoners from 5 March. The translation does not say which prison it was; Abu Salim stayed in use afterwards, and its pin records an amnesty of 426 of 530 political prisoners in March 1988, so the demolished prison may have been another.

name: Two men acquitted by an ordinary court, retried and sentenced to death, July 1983
text: Amnesty’s 1991 report says Muhammad Hilal and Mustafa al-Nawari were acquitted by an ordinary criminal court of membership of the pro-Iraqi Ba’th Party, retried by the Permanent Revolutionary Court and sentenced to death in July 1983. It says al-Nawari was ‘later executed’ and that Hilal was executed in 1984 or 1986, and that Hilal’s family was never officially told. It gives no place or cause for either. The map’s University of Tripoli hanging entry names a student, Mustafa al-Nuwairi, hanged at Benghazi University in April 1984; neither source says whether he is the Mustafa al-Nawari named here, so they are not treated as the same man. The earlier Ba’th reports of 1982 are a separate unplaced entry.

name: Deaths in Revolutionary Committees custody, June 1985, and a prisoner dead in 1986
text: The same Amnesty report says ‘Abd al-Wahid al-Zanqi and Rafiq al-Bishti allegedly died in June 1985 in the custody of members of the Revolutionary Committees, and that Husayn Hadiya Suwayd, sentenced to life in 1983 for religious activities, had reportedly died in 1986 and may have been executed. It says torture was alleged in most cases of prisoners who died in custody, but it does not give a cause for these three, and it names no prison or city. No other source was found.

name: Wanis al-‘Isawi and Hassan Nashnush held after the May 1984 attack
text: Amnesty says an oil-company employee, Wanis Idris al-‘Isawi, and a university lecturer, Hassan Nashnush, were arrested after the clash at Bab al-‘Aziziya in May 1984, were allegedly tortured and shown on television confessing to links with opposition groups abroad, and were reportedly still held without trial in Abu Salim in 1991. It gives no arrest date within May and no further detail. The prison is on the map.

name: About 2,000 arrested since February 1980, with scattered riots (CIA estimate)
text: A CIA National Intelligence Daily article of 30 May 1980, published by the State Department, says widespread arrests began in February, first of bureaucrats and then of senior military officers and members of the people’s committees, that perhaps 2,000 had been arrested and many publicly humiliated, singled out for lack of revolutionary fervour and ‘economic crimes’.
