It reports scattered local riots, perhaps four assassination attempts on Gaddafi, the latest the week before, and says he wore a bullet-proof vest and lived in a mobile command van. It also notes that death had been prescribed in April 1979 as the punishment for economic crimes. The article names no places in Tripoli.

name: Reported assassination attempt on Gaddafi, spring 1980: sources disagree on when and where
text: A National Security Council memo of 2 July 1980 says Libya watchers generally agreed that ‘some kind of assassination attempt’ on Gaddafi occurred in April 1980 and that the best guess was that he was wounded in the arm, though reports of the seriousness of the wound were probably exaggerated, and that the killings of Libyans abroad, which began in March, may have prompted it. An AFP item of 17 November 1982 in FBIS says he was wounded in the shoulder by one of his own bodyguards in an attack in Benghazi in June 1980. The month, the wound and the place do not match, and neither source places the attempt in Tripoli.

name: Reported unsuccessful mutiny in Tripoli, about June 1984
text: An FBIS report of 21 August 1984 carries an item from the Dubai newspaper Al-Bayan of 20 August, a Paris dispatch citing unnamed ‘reliable sources’, saying Gaddafi had told Sudan he was ready for reconciliation and that a ‘radical change in Libyan foreign policy and perhaps domestic policy’ had begun after ‘the unsuccessful mutiny attempt which Tripoli witnessed 2 months ago’. The item gives no date, units, place or casualties and does not say whether it means the 8 May attack on Bab al-Aziziya or a separate event. Nothing else in the files seen confirms a separate mutiny, so this is a reported, unconfirmed item.

name: Scores of suspected opponents arrested in Tripoli, and a secret detention centre in al-Hawwari, 1993
text: Amnesty’s report on 1993 says that between January and October scores of suspected government opponents were arrested in Tripoli, Benghazi and other cities, and that in October scores of military and police personnel and civilians were arrested after an ‘alleged military revolt’ in Misrata and Bani Walid, among them reportedly nine colonels. It says summary executions were reported in October but could not be confirmed and that the fate of the arrested colonels was unknown at the end of the year. It also says a police sergeant-major, ‘Ali Haroun al-Twati al-Badri, arrested in January, was believed to be held in a secret detention centre in al-Hawwari district of Tripoli. The report gives no street and does not say how many of those held were in Tripoli, so nothing is mapped. Eight men arrested after the Misrata revolt were executed on 2 January 1997 (separate entry).

name: Mustafa Bin Omran dies in custody days after his arrest, January 1984
when: Arrested 17 January 1984; family called nine days later
text: Mabrouka Kedo, the widow of Mustafa Bin Omran, told the Tarikhi oral-history project (interview of 13 April 2013) that government forces took him in on 17 January 1984 and said they would take him to Tripoli for questioning the next day. ‘Nine days later, the family received a call from the internal security offices in Tripoli’ telling them to ‘come and take his body’. She says the family does not know how he died: ‘One suggests that he was involved in a scuffle with a guard when another guard stabbed him in his neck with a rifle. Another suggests Bin Omran died of a heart attack.’ His uncles went to Tripoli, found his head wrapped in cotton and brought the body back to Benghazi for burial. The page does not say which building he was held in or where he died. This is one witness account with no official statement or post-mortem cited.

name: Women held at Abu Salim and Jdeida after the May 1984 attack
when: From mid-1984, for about four years
text: Two women told the Tarikhi project they were held after the failed 8 May 1984 raid. Amina Jornazi, interviewed in Tripoli on 11 December 2012, says she sheltered an NFSL fighter, Saleh Moadib, that arrests in her family began on a Thursday, 26 July (the year is inferred from the interview’s timeline; 26 July 1984 was a Thursday), and that she and her mother were ‘taken straight to Abu Salim prison’ and, 33 days after the arrest, to Jdaida prison. She says she and her mother were released without trial in 1988 and that others named in her account were held for 18 and 19 years and freed in 2001 and 2002. Majda Sahli, a former Tripoli University student, says she was arrested after a captured NFSL member was found with a list bearing her name, was taken blindfolded from Benghazi to a blood-stained room where dogs barked, was held in solitary confinement for 33 days, was then held at Abu Salim and at Jdaida in a cell with nine other women, and was once taken with three other inmates to a studio in Tripoli and asked to denounce their actions on camera; she served about four years. Neither page states the city for Abu Salim or Jdaida, which are in the Tripoli area (see the map entries).

name: Air force officer held at Bab al-Azizia in the late 1960s, later at ‘White Horse’ and Abu Salim, freed March 1988
text: Moftah Sharef, a former air force pilot, told the Tarikhi project (interview of 12 April 2013 in Benghazi) that he flew to Algeria during the 1967 war hoping to join the fighting in Egypt, returned to Libya in December (the page implies 1967) and was sentenced to six years: ‘I spent the first year in Bab al-Azizia and was then moved to the prison for political prisoners in Jdaida.’ If he is right, Bab al-Aziziya, later Gaddafi’s compound (see its map entry), was used to hold a prisoner under the monarchy; the page gives no year for that stay. He says he was arrested again two days after returning from Egypt in connection with the Hawwaz and Musa Ahmad conspiracy (see the December 1969 entry), spent the first 12 years of a sentence raised from one year to 13 in the ‘White Horse’ prison, later known as the Black Horse, and was then in Abu Salim, and was freed during the ‘new dawn’ of March 1988 after 18 years in prison in all. The page does not reconcile the six-year, 13-year and 18-year figures and gives no years for the arrests.

name: Anti-African violence in September–October 2000: reported killings in Tripoli and death sentences by a Tripoli tribunal
when: Late September 2000; trial date not given
text: In late September 2000 mobs attacked sub-Saharan African migrants in Libya. The worst reported violence was in Zawiya, about 40 km west of Tripoli (not mapped). Ghana’s Chronicle reported on 27 September, citing unnamed Foreign Ministry sources and an SOS telex from Ghana’s ambassador in Tripoli, that ‘scores of Ghanaians have been roasted and others beaten to death’ in Tripoli and that about 1,000 Libyans burned a Ghanaian refugee camp in Zawiya; officials gave no figure and the Tripoli claim is the newspaper’s own. A UC Davis migration-news digest summarising AFP and other reports gives an unattributed estimate of 500 dead, says thousands of Ghanaians and Nigerians were repatriated, and says Gaddafi blamed ‘enemies’ of African unity. The University of Texas SCAD database, which places the event in Zawiya, records ‘up to fifty’ foreign deaths in most media reports against seven according to the government. A Financial Times item, undated in the copy we have, which says the riots were ‘late last year’ and cites Libya’s news agency, says a tribunal in Tripoli sentenced at least seven people, two Libyans and five African migrant workers, to death and gave hundreds more prison terms. The true toll is unknown and the figures do not agree.

name: Office for Combating Heresy holding cells and Ain Zara prison, 1997
text: Abubaker Ghiryani told the Tarikhi project that he was arrested on a Monday morning in 1997, with eight cars surrounding his home before three in the morning, and taken to the holding cells of the ‘Office for Combating Heresy’, where he was interrogated and tortured. He ‘spent seven months in a solitary cell in Ain Zara’ (‘they would hang me like a roasting chicken’) before being moved to Abu Salim, which he calls torture in itself because ‘you lose all hope of knowing your fate’. In 2002 he was one of 66 prisoners accused of belonging to the Muslim Brotherhood who were found innocent and released. The number matches the 66 acquittals Amnesty reports in the Islamic Group trial (see the 16 February 2002 entry), though the page does not name the trial. His interview was recorded at Ain Zara prison on 9 December 2012. The page does not say where the Office for Combating Heresy was.

name: Mustafa Krer arrested at Tripoli airport, May 2002; his brother dies in custody
when: Arrested 2 May 2002; brother’s death notified mid-April 2002
text: Amnesty’s report of April 2004 says Mustapha Muhammad Krer was arrested on arrival at Tripoli airport on 2 May 2002 and first saw a lawyer on 15 March 2004, nearly two years later. He is charged in connection with the Libyan Islamic Fighting Group (Case 120/98) and was held for most of his detention in ‘Ayn Zara prison. He told Amnesty: ‘I returned to Libya because I believed that it was changing for the better.’ The report also says his brother, al-Mukhtar Muhammad Krer, died in custody and that the family was informed in mid-April 2002; it does not say where or how.

name: Tripoli court sentences three to death over the killing of journalist Daif al-Ghazal, July 2007
text: Daif al-Ghazal, a Libyan journalist, went missing from his home on 21 May 2005 and his body was found around 2 June in Benghazi; Libya’s justice minister said he had been shot in the head and that it was being investigated as murder (Committee to Protect Journalists). The US State Department’s report for 2008, citing Reporters Without Borders, says a Tripoli court sentenced three unnamed people to death in connection with the case in July 2007 and that Saif al-Islam al-Gaddafi conceded that officials had killed al-Ghazal but said they did so without official sanction. The killing happened outside Tripoli; the entry records the Tripoli trial only. The report says no further information was available by the end of the year.

name: Fouad Nassar al-Mahmoudi detained at Tripoli airport on his return from the UK, October 2007
text: The US State Department’s report for 2007 says security services detained Fouad Nassar al-Mahmoudi at Tripoli International Airport on 14 October on his return from the UK, that press accounts said he had come back after receiving assurances from the Libyan People’s Bureau in London, and that he remained in incommunicado detention at the end of the year. A single reported case from one source.

name: Reported attempted military coup, late November 1991
text: A JPRS report of 24 February 1992 (JPRS-NEA-92-016), reprinting an analysis of the Maghreb, says there were ‘reports from Tripoli that key changes were required after an attempted military coup late in November’ and that the appointment of Colonel Youssef Abdel Gader al-Dabri as intelligence head, a former Free Officer and a southerner, followed a ‘clear-out of northerners, including civilian security officials’. It does not say where the attempt happened, who took part or whether anyone was killed, and no other file seen confirms it, so it is a reported item only.

name: Rixos Al Nasr Hotel and Convention Centre
text: A hotel and conference complex that housed foreign journalists in 2011, was a loyalist stronghold during the fall of Tripoli, and later became the seat of the General National Congress. On 4 March 2011 foreign journalists, about 130 invited by the government, were barred from leaving the hotel without a minder. By 22 August, as the rebels entered Tripoli, loyalists still held it. Roughly 40 foreigners, mostly journalists, were kept inside, and Al Jazeera said they were being used as human shields. Saif al-Islam Gaddafi appeared at the hotel in the early hours of 23 August. The journalists were released in Red Cross vans around 24 August. The Timeline of Tripoli says the General National Congress began meeting in the 'Ghabat Al Nasr Convention Centre' in 2012. The High Council of State occupied the former GNC headquarters at the Rixos Al Nasr Convention Centre on 22 April 2016, and GNC loyalists attacked it on 10 October 2016. It was seized again in October 2016, besieged in March 2017, and a Reuters report dated 24 May 2019 says rockets hit the Rixos hotel. No coordinates were found in any source seen. The sources use two names (Ghabat Al Nasr and Rixos Al Nasr) and it is not confirmed that they are the same building.

name: Undeclared nuclear-programme sites (Al Hashan, Al-Khalla, Salah Eddin)
text: Group of sites near Tripoli that Libya disclosed in 2003-04 as hosting its undeclared nuclear programme; later cleared by US, UK and IAEA teams. NTI's IAEA-based summary names Al-Hashan (operated 1997-2002), Al-Khalla (its successor), Salah Eddin, Janzour, Sawani, Al-Karamia and El-Ezeizia as undeclared sites, plus underground storage at Sabha. Wikipedia says that in October 2000 a single complete device was installed at Al Hashan. Exact addresses are not published in the pages seen. Libya's 19 December 2003 announcement ended its nuclear weapons efforts. The IAEA verified the sites in 2004, and NTI reports that the US and UK worked with the IAEA to remove all nuclear-related equipment and materials in three stages, with the most sensitive items first and the work done by September 2004. The IAEA then reported on the programme to its Board. The pages seen do not describe the present state of these buildings. Equipment was removed in 2004, so no weapons-related material is reported to remain, but the sites' current use is not documented here. This is the overview of the group. IAEA GOV/2004/12 Annex I lists the declared sites as A Al Hashan, B Al Fallah, C Al Khalla, D Salah Eddin, E Janzour (machine shop), F Sabha (yellowcake store), G Sawani (initial storage), H Al Karamia, I Tajura (desalination plant), J the National Board of Scientific Research headquarters, K Al Ezeizia and L the Tajura Nuclear Research Centre. The IAEA gives place names only, with no addresses or coordinates, so the pins for A-D, H and K are suburb-level; Janzour, Sawani and Tajura were already on the map. The Sabha store and the NBSR headquarters are not mapped.

name: 1 September 1969 coup in Tripoli (radio station and barracks)
text: The overnight coup that ended the monarchy; in Tripoli, officers seized the radio station, barracks, anti-aircraft batteries and airports. On 1 September 1969 Free Officers under Gaddafi staged a coup while King Idris was in Turkey for treatment, launching in Benghazi and finishing within two hours. In Tripoli, Khweldi Hameidi captured the radio station, Umar Muhayshi took over the barracks, and Abdessalam Jalloud seized the anti-aircraft batteries. The officers also occupied airports, police depots and government offices. Hameidi was sent to arrest Crown Prince Hasan ar-Rida and make him renounce his claim. Military control of Tripoli was established within a few days. Gaddafi ended the monarchy and proclaimed a republic. The queen's private secretary was placed under house probation by officers led by Omar Almheishi and later released after negotiations, by her own account. Idris went into exile in Egypt and was sentenced to death in absentia in 1971. The pages opened give no addresses for the radio station or barracks, and the Wheelus connection is not documented. A memoir by the queen's secretary is a personal account. The 'police depots' are named without saying which force held them; no source opened says they were Military Police, and the Military Police Command compound is documented only from the 1980s (see its own profile). No coordinates are given.

name: Piazza Italia / Independence Square / Green Square / Martyrs' Square
text: The central square beside the Red Castle that has changed names with each regime. The Italians built it on the site of the old bread market (souq al-khubs) and expanded it several times in the 1930s; Florestano Di Fausto designed the square around the castle. After independence in 1951 it was called Independence Square. Streets meeting there include Omar Mukhtar Avenue, Independence Street (leading to King Idris's palace), 24 December Avenue and Mizran Street. A large fountain designed by an Italian architect stood at its centre, and a seafront avenue is marked by two tall pillars. After 1969 it was renamed Green Square after the Green Book. The Royal Miramare Theatre, opposite the Red Castle, was demolished by his government after the 1960s to make room for mass rallies. Protests took place there on 20 and 25 March 2011. Rebels took it on 21-22 August 2011 and renamed it Martyrs' Square; crowds celebrated there on 31 August and 2 September. No coordinates were seen on any page opened. It lies directly in front of the Red Castle entrance, but no exact centre is given.

name: Libyan state TV headquarters (Al-Jamahiriya TV)
text: The Tripoli headquarters of Libya's state broadcaster, which carried Gaddafi-era government coverage and was struck by NATO in 2011. Station building work in Tripoli and Benghazi began in 1967 and finished by the end of 1968; regular television started on 24 December 1968. Under Gaddafi it was renamed from the People's Revolutionary Broadcasting Corporation to the Libyan Jamahiriya Broadcasting Corporation on 24 December 2001. The main channel, Al-Jamahiriya, covered People's Congress sessions and readings of the Green Book. It reached the Arab world and Europe by satellite from 1997. On 30 July 2011 NATO struck the state TV's Tripoli headquarters and two installations; the broadcaster said three journalists died and 21 were hurt. Loyalists took refuge at the TV centre on 20 August 2011, and the channels went off air by 21-22 August as rebels took the building. The corporation was dissolved. A relaunched channel later broadcast from Cairo. The exact street address of the 2011 headquarters is not given in the sources seen; no coordinates. Casualty figures come from the broadcaster and were unverified.

name: Al-Fatah missile project
text: Libya's domestic ballistic missile development effort of the 1990s, publicly reported but with no confirmed location in the sources used. Reports summarised by GlobalSecurity and Wikipedia say Libya sought to build a domestic missile (reported range 950-1,000 km), drawing on earlier OTRAG work in the desert near Sebha from 1979. Foreign help from Iraq, Iran, Serbia and China was alleged. A test facility is mentioned but not located. Per GlobalSecurity, 1995 reports said Iraqi technicians were working on Al Fatah, and in 1999 US imagery satellites reportedly photographed an enlarged Al Fatah test facility. Reports of North Korean talks later proved false after 2003. In December 2003 Libya agreed to eliminate missiles beyond 300 km range and 500 kg payload. Libya largely abandoned the programme in 2004 in exchange for sanctions relief, per Wikipedia. No site is known to remain; nothing in the sources opened describes its present state. Still no confirmed location. GlobalSecurity says only that US imagery in 1999 showed a missile test facility being enlarged 'as part of the Al-Fatah development program', without saying where. The closest documented candidate is the Jarmah launch site (now on the map): built by OTRAG from 1980, it was described by CIA imagery in December 1983 as 'currently being used by the Libyans for the development of a short-range missile'. No source says Jarmah is the Al-Fatah site, which was a later (1990s) effort, so it stays unpinned. A 1989 report of a desert camp about 100 km from Sebha is a second unplaced clue.

name: Sabha yellowcake store and 2011 chemical stock reports
text: Post-2011 concerns about Libyan stockpiles at Sabha (uranium ore concentrate) and chemical stocks reported in the Jufra area; far from Tripoli. NTI lists underground yellowcake storage at Sabha as one of the undeclared sites disclosed in 2004. The IAEA visited it and in December 2011 recommended a quick sale and transfer, warning that storage conditions were worsening. In 2013, the UN said 6,400 barrels were stored near Sabha. In September-November 2011 rebels and press reported chemical stocks near Jufra, and Libya told the OPCW on 1 November 2011 that more suspected stocks had been found. An OPCW team confirmed the declared mustard stockpile at Ruwagha intact in November 2011. On 9 December 2013 the UN's Tarek Mitri said an IAEA team would verify the Sabha stockpile. The pages seen do not give the present state. The 2013 account says the barrels remained under a Libyan army battalion at a former military installation near Sabha. No coordinates (Sabha is in the far south, well outside the 100 km range; distance not stated in the sources, so null). I did not find a source seen for the Misrata or 2011 Rabta claims in the brief, so they are not covered. Jufra reports are press claims.

name: Libyan Scud / short-range missile units
text: Libya's Soviet- and North Korean-supplied short-range missiles; unit and storage locations near Tripoli, Sirte, Sebha and Al-Jufra are not published in the sources used. GlobalSecurity says Libya obtained Scud-B and FROG-7 missiles from the Soviet Union in the mid-1970s. GlobalSecurity also refers to North Korean Scud-C missiles. OpenStreetMap lists an 'Artillery and Missile School' near Tripoli at 32.766 N, 13.197 E, though no source ties it to Scuds. Two Scuds were fired at Lampedusa in April 1986 after the US raid. After the 19 December 2003 deal, Libya agreed to remove missiles over 300 km range, so it gave up Scud-C but not 300 km Scud-B, per GlobalSecurity. In 2011 Libyan forces reportedly fired Scud-B at rebel areas and missed; NATO strikes reportedly destroyed the rest. Not documented in the pages seen; some missiles are believed to have survived outside government control after 2011 but no source opened confirms this. CIA imagery now locates two Scud sites. The first confirmed Scud-B launcher (April 1977) was at the Tarabulus Military Storage Area Southeast, 32°49′45″N 13°20′26″E; elements of two brigades and at least 21 launchers were at Bin Ghashir, 32°45′30″N 13°12′30″E, in 1982. The 1980 report also names Tajura South barracks, Madaniyah barracks, a barracks and vehicle storage depot, Kulliyat, and two brigades at Benghazi, but gives no coordinates for them in the text we hold; the very first Scuds (July 1976) were seen at the Al Aziziyah ammunition depot. The only reported 2011 launch position is the first Scud of the war, about 80 km east of Sirte (also on the map).

name: Tripoli air-defence network (1986)
text: Libya's surface-to-air missile network around Tripoli, suppressed in the 1986 US raid; individual sites are not publicly located in the sources used. The account of the 1986 raid cited on Wikipedia says Libyan defences in the whole country included four S-200 (SA-5) units and 86 S-75/S-125 (SA-2/SA-3) units, with Tripoli alone also holding SA-6, SA-8 and Crotale units. Individual battery locations around Tripoli are not given. In April 1986 US A-7E and F/A-18A aircraft fired anti-radar missiles at air defence networks in Tripoli and Benghazi while EF-111s and EA-6Bs jammed radars. The account says no SAM launches homed on US aircraft, and one SA-6 tracked an A-6, which evaded it. Libya claimed five major radars destroyed; this is a Libyan claim. Libya's air defences were again targeted by NATO in 2011. The pages seen do not state which sites survive, whether any are reused, or what their condition is today. No coordinates or distance: location approximate and not published for individual batteries. The 'SA-5 near Tripoli' positions are widely repeated but I did not find a source with locations; treat as unverified.

name: University of Libya, Tripoli faculties (1957)
text: The Tripoli branch of the first Libyan university, which began with a Faculty of Science. The University of Libya began in 1957 and its Tripoli branch started with the Faculty of Science, one of the first practical colleges in the country. The Faculty of Agriculture was added in 1966. After the 1969 coup the Tripoli and Benghazi campuses were subject to a crackdown. A college of petroleum and minerals was added in 1972. In 1973 the University of Libya split into Tripoli and Benghazi universities, and in 1976 Tripoli was renamed Al Fateh University after student unrest that April. Political activity was heavily restricted from the early 1970s; by the late 1970s opponents could be arrested. The medical school was ordered to admit about 2,000 students against a capacity of roughly 150. Renamed University of Tripoli in 2012. The present main campus is in south-east Tripoli at about 32.856 N, 13.221 E. The original 1957 site of the Faculty of Science is not stated, so no coordinates are given. The campus coordinates (32°51'21"N 13°13'17"E) are the later university, not necessarily the 1957 building.

name: Dar Bishi Synagogue
text: A synagogue in the old Jewish Quarter that was the focus of a short-lived reopening in 2011. Dar Bishi stood in the Hara Kebira, the old Jewish Quarter of the medina. Tripoli had about 14,000 Jews in 1903, and in 1941 Jews were about a quarter of the city, with 44 synagogues. Rioters in November 1945 looted nearly all the city's synagogues and destroyed five. Italy's racial laws from 1938 removed Jews from public office and state schools. Most Jews left after 1948 and 1967. After 1969 Jewish property was confiscated and fewer than 40 Jews remained by 1972. Diarna says the last member of the Jewish community died in 2003 (another source says the last Jew was allowed to leave that year). In 2011 David Gerbi began clearing the building and reopened it for prayer, but work stopped on 8 October 2011 after protests. Condition and ownership unknown; Diarna made a 3D digital reconstruction. Foundation date and its exact street are not given in sources opened. Wikipedia says Gerbi removed a brick wall blocking the entrance. Later reports of conversion or demolition were not verified, so no coordinates are given.

name: Banco di Roma and Banco di Napoli buildings
text: Branches of the first Italian banks in Tripoli, plus the Bank of Italy headquarters of the 1920s. Banco di Roma was the first Italian bank in Tripoli, opening in 1907. Banco di Napoli received authority for a Tripoli branch in December 1911, and its Tripoli building stood on Corso Vittorio Emanuele; its sources date the opening to 1913 or to an inauguration on 30 November 1930. The Bank of Italy building went up in the 1920s under governor De Bono. The Banco di Roma building is also marked on a tourist map of the old city, and directions to the Othman Pasha madrasa say to walk toward the Banco di Roma from Bab al-Bahr. On 13 November 1969 the Libyan government nationalised Banco di Napoli and turned it into a Libyan joint-stock company. Its Tripoli operations had resumed fully in 1952 after British oversight began in 1946. The Italian community was expelled in 1970. Exact addresses and architects are not given in the sources opened. Which present building is the Banco di Roma is unconfirmed, so no coordinates. Banco di Napoli operations resumed in 1952 after British oversight in 1946.

name: Libya's 2003 disarmament deal and 2004 removals
text: Libya's December 2003 decision to end its weapons programmes and the 2004 US-UK-IAEA removals from sites around Tripoli. On 19 December 2003 Gaddafi announced Libya would voluntarily end its nuclear, chemical and long-range missile efforts. US and UK inspection teams had visited sites in October and December 2003. This is a national event, so no single location is mapped. The IAEA, with US and UK help, removed nuclear-related equipment and materials in three stages, completing the work in September 2004 (per NTI). Highly enriched uranium fuel left Tajoura for Russia in March 2004. Libya joined the Chemical Weapons Convention in early 2004 and made its first declaration; sanctions relief followed. Libya's weapons programmes were declared dismantled. After 2011 the sites were left lightly guarded; the OPCW found the Ruwagha stockpile intact in November 2011. No location; the exact number of visited sites varies by account (GlobalSecurity cites 10 in one account and dozens in others). Dates on the Chemical Weapons Convention entry differ between 6 January and 5 February 2004 in Wikipedia.

name: Italian colonist villages around Tripoli
text: Planned agricultural settlements founded for Italian farming families, some of them near Tripoli. Italian colonists concentrated in the farmland around Tripoli. In 1938 Italy founded 26 agricultural villages for about 20,000 colonists, including Gioda, Crispi, Olivetti and Breviglieri. Settlers had to come from large families, pass medical and background checks, and have a household head in the Fascist party. The Tripoli area held the largest Italian community in the colony: 47,400 Italians among 113,212 residents in 1939. In January 1939 the coastal areas became part of metropolitan Italy. In 1970 Gaddafi ordered the expulsion of about 20,000 remaining Italians and nationalised Italian companies. Their property was confiscated, valued at about 3 billion euros today. The Italian population had fallen to about 1,500 by 1986. The exact locations of the villages near Tripoli were not given in sources opened, so no coordinates. Wikipedia says most of the farming villages were in Cyrenaica. The internment camps of the 1930s were in Cyrenaica, not Tripoli, so none are listed here.

name: Lampedusa missile attack launch site (April 1986)
text: Libya's missile reprisal on 15 April 1986 against the US Coast Guard LORAN station on Lampedusa, Italy; launch site often said to be near Sirte but not confirmed. The reprisal followed Operation El Dorado Canyon. Wikipedia says Libya fired two Scud missiles at the NATO base at Capo Ponente, Lampedusa, at about 16:33 UTC on 15 April 1986. One exploded about 2 km northwest and the other about 2 km southwest of the base, in the sea. Libya later said it targeted a US-led NATO base, not Italy. The attack caused a diplomatic crisis with Italy. The page seen does not state the launch site; reports that it was near Sirte, east of Tripoli, were not confirmed in the sources I opened. Lampedusa is unchanged and is today an Italian island; the launch location remains unrecorded in the sources used here, and no site is mapped. Launch site still not published: the Italian and English accounts say only that the two Scuds came from Libya and landed about 2 km north-west and south-west of the Capo Ponente (35°31′N 12°31′E) base. 'Sirte' is common in press but unconfirmed, so no pin.

name: Royal Miramare Theatre
text: The largest theatre in Tripoli, a 2,000-seat Italian opera house opposite the Red Castle, now demolished. Opened in 1925 as the Real Teatro Miramare during the governorship of Emilio De Bono; Wikipedia's timeline lists it with 1928 buildings. It seated 2,000 and staged operas, including Verdi's Un ballo in maschera, and hosted Italian and European companies. It stood opposite the Corniche, across from the Red Castle. Allied bombing in World War II heavily damaged it, and it was still maintained until independence. Wikipedia says Gaddafi's government demolished it after the 1960s to make room for large demonstrations in what became Green Square. A Libyan blog instead says it was demolished in the late 1960s, before the coup. Gone. A 2018 lecture on its history was held at Dar Hassan al-Faqih in Tripoli. Demolition date (late 1960s vs after 1969) and architect are not settled. No coordinates are given.

name: Hara Kebira (Jewish Quarter)
text: The historic Jewish quarter inside the Old City, where Dar Bishi and many other synagogues stood. Hara Kebira ("great quarter") was the main Jewish neighbourhood of the Old City. Jews ran many shops in nearby Souq al-Turk and Souq al-Hrara in the Italian period. The Alliance Israélite counted about 14,000 Jews in Tripoli in 1903; in 1941 they were 25 percent of the population with 44 synagogues. The 1945 riots (5-7 November) left about 4,000 Jews homeless. Violence in June 1948 killed 12 more, and after the 1967 war over 6,000 were evacuated to Rome. After the 1969 coup Jewish property was confiscated and debts owed to Jews were cancelled. Jewish men were arrested, and fewer than 40 Jews remained by 1972. One account says the last Jew, an elderly woman, was allowed to leave in 2003. Exact boundaries of the quarter were not documented in the sources opened. Its present occupants and condition are unknown.

name: Grand Hotel of Tripoli (Italian original)
text: A large Italian-era seafront hotel of 350 rooms near the cathedral, later demolished and replaced. Designed by Florestano Di Fausto in 1920 according to a Libyan blog, though Wikipedia's timeline lists the Grand Hotel under 1925 and says it may date from 1924. It stood in an open park overlooking the port near what is now the Algerian Embassy and the Gamal Abdel Nasser (former cathedral) Mosque. The hotel had 350 rooms and was known for its many arches. It sits next to the Al Waddan Hotel. The blog says the original was demolished in the 1980s and a new hotel on the same site was designed by a British company in 1982. The exterior wall of the new building shows a picture of the original. The new hotel was deserted after 2011 according to the blog. Design year (1920) and opening year (1924/1925) differ; the demolition date and the 1982 rebuilding come from one blog citing a Facebook group. Corinthia Hotel Tripoli (2003) is a different building. No coordinates found.

name: Dar Bishi Synagogue
text: The last surviving synagogue in the Old City, designed in 1922 by Umberto Di Segni and now derelict. The old city once had about 33 synagogues; Dar Bishi is the only one still standing. In the 1980s the Libyan government tried to restore it but abandoned the effort. Tripoli's last indigenous Jewish community member died in 2003. In 2011 Libyan Jewish exile David Gerbi returned, cleared debris and reopened it for prayer, but on 8 October 2011 protests forced the work onto indefinite hold and he was urged to leave. The building is in very poor shape, with refuse on the floors and most windows bricked up; some parts have been demolished. Reports suggest local authorities planned to turn it into an Islamic library. No coordinates found. It lies in the Hara Kebira (old Jewish quarter) of the Old City. The Islamic library plan is a report, not confirmed.

name: Tripoli International Fair
text: The oldest trade fair in Africa, founded by the Italian colonial government. Founded by the Italian government in 1927 and promoted alongside the Tripoli Grand Prix to showcase Italian Libya. In the 1930s it was one of the main international fairs of the colonial world; the 1934 fair became known for a first air trip across an oasis of the Libyan Sahara, commemorated by an Italian stamp. The most notable structure is a symbolic monument at the entrance, the Pavilion of the Governorate of Rome, by the Egyptian-born Italian architect Alessandro Limongelli. After World War II the fair reopened on a much smaller scale. The 2008 edition ran 2-12 April and in 2010 over 1,000 participants from 29 countries took part. The fairground location, its Gaddafi-era role, and whether the pavilion survives were not found, so no coordinates.

name: Jamahiriya institutions: People's Committees and Revolutionary Committees
text: The state system of Gaddafi's Jamahiriya, run from Tripoli through committees and congresses rather than ministries. People's Committees began around 1973 in the cultural revolution, organised by function (universities, firms, media) and geography, with over 2,000 by mid-1973. The General People's Congress (1977) replaced the Revolutionary Command Council, and the General People's Committee replaced the cabinet, with 'secretaries' instead of ministers. Revolutionary Committees, organised from 1977, supervised the system, surveyed the population, repressed opposition and ran public executions; in 1979 they took control of Basic People's Congress elections. The system ended with the Jamahiriya in October 2011. This is a system, not a single building; no committee office locations were found.

name: People's Hall (General People's Congress)
text: The large hall where the General People's Congress met under Gaddafi. Protesters set it on fire in February 2011 and it later burned repeatedly. Built in the late 1970s or early 1980s, it hosted the General People's Congress and was normally closed to the public. Demonstrators set it on fire on 21 February 2011 and it was reignited on 22 February and burned out, along with other government buildings including the Justice Ministry at Martyrs' Square. In March 2016 militia commander Haithem Tajouri's brigade took over the hall; it was later abandoned, used by gangs, and set on fire several times, most recently on 13 April 2017. The Libyan Heritage House lists it as destroyed following the 2011 revolution. No coordinates were found; exact location is not given on the pages seen. Current condition is not documented.

name: Central Bank of Libya headquarters
text: The headquarters in Tripoli of Libya's central bank, which began as the National Bank of Libya in 1956. The bank was set up by a 1955 law and began operating on 1 April 1956 as the National Bank of Libya. It became the Bank of Libya in 1963 and took its present name after the 1969 coup. The sources seen do not describe the building itself or events at it between 1969 and 2011. The bank's administration split during the 2011 civil war and again from 2014, and it announced reunification in August 2023. In August 2024 the Tripoli government removed governor Sadiq al-Kabir, prompting the east-based government to close oil fields; Naji Belqasem has been governor since October 2024. The building's address and any damage in conflicts are not documented in the sources seen; no coordinates.

name: Lungomare Conte Volpi (the Corniche)
text: The Italian-built waterfront boulevard along the harbour, laid out under governor Giuseppe Volpi. Giuseppe Volpi governed Tripolitania from 1921 to 1925 and hired architect Armando Brasini to lead its renovation, including the waterfront boulevard. Wikipedia's timeline dates the Lungomare Conte Volpi to 1924. A Columbia University lantern-slide record shows it as "Il Lungomare Conte Volpi" in the early 20th century. The promenade was once considered among the most beautiful on the Mediterranean. In the 1970s a road expansion project filled in a long stretch of the sea, so the Corniche has no sea in front of it; the Red Castle also lost its sea frontage and Saraya Lake formed. The extent of the original waterfront is not mapped here, so no point is given. Brasini's role is stated in a blog.

name: Police college (Tripoli, location not published)
text: A police training college whose cadets graduated in Tripoli; a Human Rights Watch report also lists a Police Academy among Tripoli sites used in a Muslim Brotherhood retrial. Libyan state news (JANA) reported on 4 September 1985, during the 16th anniversary celebrations of the 1969 revolution, a ceremony for the graduation of the 10th batch of the police college. The director spoke of training cadets to be ideologically committed to the revolution's goals, and the secretary of the General People's Committee for Justice attended. Human Rights Watch (2006) lists the Police Academy among Tripoli sites in connection with a retrial of Muslim Brotherhood defendants. None of the sources opened gives an address, so it is not mapped. It is not shown to be the same as the 1969 'police depots' or the Military Police Command. The 2006 HRW detail comes from a summary of its report, not a page read in full here.

name: Tripoli Central Station and the Tripoli-Tajura line
text: The Italian-built station that began three narrow-gauge lines, including a 21 km line east to Tajura. Tripoli Central was the start of three Italian lines: Tripoli-Zuara (118 km), Tripoli-Garian (90 km) and Tripoli-Tagiura (21 km, ten stations). They used 950 mm gauge, and Gurgi and Gargaresc were the first two stops on the Zuara and Garian lines. Italy built nearly 400 km of railway in Libya and none after 1926. After the 1911 Ain Zara battle the Italians built a line linking that oasis to Tripoli. A Tripoli-Benghazi line begun in 1941 was never finished. Wikipedia lists Tripoli Central station among the Italian-era buildings later demolished, without a date. Opening years for each line, the tramway named in the request, and the station site are not documented in the sources opened; no coordinates are given.

name: Karamanli Mosque (Ahmed Pasha Karamanli Mosque)
text: An 18th-century mosque complex founded by Ahmed Pasha Karamanli, founder of the Karamanli dynasty, with a madrasa and family tombs. A source places it in the Souq al-Mushir area. Ahmed Karamanli (1686-1745) seized power in Tripoli in the 1711 coup and made the governorship hereditary. Construction of the mosque began in 1736 and the complex includes a madrasa and the tombs of dynasty members. The sources seen say nothing about the mosque in 1969-2011. The mosque is listed as active. It was vandalised in 2014 during the civil conflict, damaging its ceramic tiles and marble decoration, and UNESCO condemned the attack. Whether repairs were made is not stated. No coordinates were found. The sources seen do not say whether Ahmed Pasha's own tomb is in the complex.

name: Ahmed Pasha Karamanli Mosque
text: The mosque, madrasa and dynastic mausoleum founded by Ahmed Karamanli, near the clock tower and Souq al-Mushir. Ahmed Karamanli, founder of the dynasty that ruled from 1711, began the mosque in 1736. Another source gives 1736-1738. It has 25 domes, a madrasa and a mausoleum for members of the family. It stands beside Souq al-Mushir, next to the Red Castle, and a 1994 photograph shows it framed with the clock tower through a souq gate. The Karamanlis ruled Tripolitania until the Ottomans removed them in 1835. In 2014, during fighting in Libya, the mosque was vandalised and its ceramic tiles and marble decoration were damaged; UNESCO condemned the attack. No coordinates were seen on any page opened. Completion date and any Italian or Gaddafi-era restoration were not found.

name: 1945 anti-Jewish riots in Tripoli (sites)
text: The 5-7 November 1945 riots under British military administration, in which synagogues and Jewish homes in Tripoli were attacked. The riots ran from 5 to 7 November 1945 in Tripolitania, then under British occupation, after a wave of rioting on 2 November in Aleppo and Cairo. In Tripoli, 38 people were killed; the toll across the region was over 140, including 36 children. Rioters looted nearly all of Tripoli's synagogues and destroyed five, and plundered over 1,000 Jewish homes and businesses. About 4,000 Jews were left homeless. The British were criticised for responding slowly; at least 550 Muslims were arrested and tried in British military courts. Which streets and synagogues in Tripoli were hit is not named in the sources opened, so no coordinates are given. The page's town totals add to 135 not "more than 140". Villages such as Amrus (40 killed), Zanzur (34), Tajura (7) and Zawia (13) were also hit. Further riots in June 1948 killed 12.

name: 1967 Six-Day War riots in Tripoli
text: The June 1967 anti-Jewish and anti-Western riots that triggered the departure of most of the remaining Jewish community. On 15 June 1967 Libyan youths held violent demonstrations backing the Arab states at war with Israel, which led to the deaths of many Jews and the destruction of US and British property. Wikipedia says the unrest included attacks on US and British embassies and oil company offices. After the war, anti-Jewish violence killed 18. King Idris allowed Jews to leave temporarily, and the Italian Navy helped evacuate over 6,000 of them to Rome within a month. About 7,000 remaining Jews were evacuated overall, according to another page. The pages opened do not say which of these attacks were in Tripoli, or name particular buildings. Casualty figures differ. No coordinates are given.

name: Bab al-Bahr (Sea Gate)
text: The harbour-side gate of the Old City, giving its name to the quarter around the Dragut and Gurgi mosques. Bab al-Bahr opens from the old city toward the harbour. Dragut, killed at Malta in 1565, was buried in the nearby Sidi Darghut Mosque, close to this gate. The Gurgi Mosque (1834) is in the Bab al-Bahr district near the sea, and the Othman Pasha madrasa (1654) lies on the central axis running from the seafront into the city. The date of the gate itself, and any Italian-era changes, were not found in the sources opened. Visitors reach the medina from here; its present state is not documented in the sources opened. No coordinates were seen on a page I opened, and the gate does not appear in the OpenStreetMap extract, so none are given. Gate date is unknown.

name: Souq al-Turk
text: One of the longest markets of the Old City, a covered and open street that became a showcase for fine textiles and jewellery. Created by an Ottoman governor and named for its resemblance to open markets in Turkey. It lies in two connected parts, one covered opposite the clock tower and one open. Under the Italians its character shifted from oriental to western European, and it was crowded on Sundays. Traders were mostly Jewish, with some Italians, Indians and Africans. Jewish families ran toy and sewing shops there. Nearby Souq al-Hrara sold silk and was also mostly Jewish-run. Which governor founded it and when is not clear; the source names a "Wali Mohamed Bahsa" with a doubtful spelling. Souq al-Rabaa was not found in sources opened. No coordinates.

name: Central Bank of Libya
text: Libya's central bank, in the former Savings Bank building on Al Fatah Street, designed in 1921 by Armando Brasini. Founded 1955 as the National Bank of Libya and opened 1 April 1956; renamed Bank of Libya in 1963 and Central Bank of Libya after the 1969 coup. In March 2011 governor Farhat Bengdara resigned and joined the rebels, first arranging for most external assets to be frozen. The bank split in the civil wars; the Tripoli and Bayda branches agreed to unify in 2021 and announced reunification in August 2023. Naji Belqasem has been governor since 3 October 2024. No coordinates found.

name: Hammam Dragut (Darghouth Turkish Bath)
text: An Ottoman bath attached to the Dragut Mosque and tomb in the Old City. The bath is annexed to the Sidi Darghut Mosque and tomb. Wikipedia dates it to 1081 AH (1670-71). Its timeline separately lists an Iskandar Pasha hammam built in 1604, and the mosque page says Iskander Pasha built or renovated a bath in the early 1600s. The old-city map from a travel site names three hammams: Hammam Darghut, Hammam al-Kebira and Hammam Alheygha. A Manchester research record also covers the surviving historic hammams of the medina. Present use is not stated in the sources opened. Whether the 1604 Iskandar Pasha bath and the 1670-71 Darghouth bath are the same building is unclear. No coordinates were found.

name: Fort Hamidiye and Fort Sultaniye (1911 landing)
text: The two Ottoman harbour forts shelled by the Italian fleet on 3-4 October 1911. Starting at 15:30 on 3 October 1911 an Italian squadron fired on Forts Hamidiye and Sultaniye from about 9,500 m, then closer, leaving the forts badly damaged; the Ottoman gunboat Seyyad and the steamer Derna were scuttled. Captain Umberto Cagni's naval landing force went ashore on 5 October, took Fort Sultaniye and raised the Italian flag at noon, while sappers took Fort Hamidiye. By 16:30 troops reached the marketplace. Italian strength in the city rose to about 35,000 by 11 October. Neither fort was matched to a surviving building or to an OpenStreetMap feature; no coordinates are given. The Wikipedia battle page shows the city centre only.

name: Bab Jedid (New Gate) and Bab Zanata
text: A western gate of the Old City opened in the 1860s to replace the earlier Bab Zanata. Bab Zanata was blocked during the civil war of 1831 under Ali II Karamanli. An inscription dated 12 February 1865 says residents asked the Ottoman governor to open a new gate in its place, and it became known as Bab Jedid, the New Gate. Wikipedia's timeline dates the opening of Bab el-Jedid to 1860, so sources differ on the year. The gate sits on the western side of the old city. One of the main gates of the medina according to the page opened; present condition not documented. Year (1860 vs 1865) differs between sources. It is not stated whether Bab al-Hurriya (Freedom Gate) is the same as Bab Jedid. No coordinates were found.

name: Uthman Pasha Madrasa
text: A 17th-century Quranic school beside the Dragut Mosque that still teaches. Founded in 1654 under Ottoman rule and named for the governor Othman Pasha al-Saqizli. It lies in the Bab al-Bahr area near the Dragut entrance, on the axis leading from the sea into the city. A square courtyard leads to more than ten marble rooms under two Ottoman domes, and a courtyard shows inscriptions and Ottoman taps. Mohammed Kamel Ben Mustafa, born in 1828 in Zawiya, studied and taught there. Still operating as a religious school with study circles, according to a 2020s article. Whether Othman Pasha personally paid for it is not stated. No coordinates were found.

name: Tripoli International Fair
text: A trade fair ground on Omar Mukhtar Avenue, founded by the Italians in 1927 and described as the oldest trade fair in Africa. Founded in 1927 by the Italian government and used in the 1930s to promote Italian Libya; its entrance monument, the Pavilion of Rome, was designed by Alessandro Limongelli. It reopened at reduced scale after the Second World War. The 2008 session ran 2-12 April; in 2010 more than 1,000 participants from 29 countries took part, organised by the General Board of Fairs. The sources seen do not describe the site after 2010. No coordinates were found. Events in 2011 and the present state are not documented in the sources seen.

name: Souq al-Mushir
text: An open-air market street named for the Ottoman governor Rajab Pasha, running from the Huwara souq toward the clock tower. Built by the Ottoman governor Rajab Pasha, who ruled Tripoli in 1906-1908, and named for his title al-Mushir. It runs from the opening of Souq al-Huwara on the south-east toward the clock tower. It originally sold flowers, medicinal herbs and gardening supplies. The Karamanli Mosque stands on it. A timeline gives 1935 for the souq's reconstruction under the Italians. Now sells clothes, household goods, food and hardware. The Italian reconstruction of 1935 is listed only in one timeline. OpenStreetMap maps a gate called Bab al-Mushir near the Red Castle, but the souq itself has no coordinates here.

name: Benghazi basketball stadium (televised hanging, 5 June 1984; outside Tripoli)
text: The venue of the best-known televised hanging under Gaddafi, in Benghazi rather than Tripoli. On 5 June 1984 Al-Sadek Hamed Al-Shuwehdy was publicly executed at the end of a show trial held in a basketball stadium in Benghazi, in front of students; the event had been announced as the trial of one of Gaddafi's political enemies. Other hangings of that period were broadcast and re-broadcast on Libyan state television. In Tripoli, the hanging of a student on the University of Tripoli campus in April 1984 is on the map as its own entry. The stadium is not named in the pages opened and lies outside Greater Tripoli, so it is not mapped. No source opened places a similar stadium hanging in Tripoli itself.

name: Old City gates (Bab al-Bahr, Bab Zanata, Bab Hawwara, Bab el-Jedid)
text: The historic gates of the walled Old City: Bab al-Bahr on the sea side, Bab Hawwara to the south-east, Bab Zenata to the west, and the later Bab el-Jedid. Wikipedia names Bab al-Bahr (north, near the sea), Bab Hawwara (south-east, probably today's Bab al-Mensha) and Bab Zenata (west, originally Bab al-Ashdar). The Timeline of Tripoli says Bab el-Jedid opened in 1860. Only sections of the walls remain. The sources seen give no events at the gates between 1969 and 2011. Only sections of the city walls survive. Individual gate positions were not found, so no coordinates are given. Bab Darghouth has its own entry.

name: Sidi Salem Mosque
text: An old mosque of the medina that predates the Spanish conquest and was restored in the Ottoman period. Wikipedia dates Sidi Salem to the late 15th century with a restoration in 1670. That places it before the Spanish conquest of 1510, the Knights' rule from 1530 and the Ottoman capture of 1551. Its timeline repeats the 1670 restoration. It is one of the older religious buildings of the old city alongside the Naqa Mosque. No founder or architectural description was found in the pages opened. Location within the medina, founder and later history are not documented in the sources opened. No coordinates are given.

name: Libyan Jamahiriya Broadcasting Corporation / Al-Jamahiriya TV
text: The state broadcaster of the Jamahiriya, strictly controlled by the state, with its headquarters in Tripoli. NATO struck the Tripoli headquarters of Al-Jamahiriya and two of its installations on 30 July 2011; the station said three journalists were killed and 21 wounded, which was not independently verified. NATO said the aim was to stop 'terror broadcasts'. Al-Jamahiriya, Al Urubah and Al-Shababiyah went off air in late August 2011. Later organisation not researched. No coordinates found for the headquarters; the radio buildings were not documented.

name: Souq al-Mushir
text: An open-air market in the Old City named for the Ottoman governor Rajab Pasha, running between the Huwara souq and the clock tower. A local source says it was built under al-Wali al-Mushir Rajab Pasha between 1906 and 1908; the Timeline of Tripoli says it was reconstructed in 1935. It includes the Karamanli mosque and sells clothing, household goods, food and hardware today. The sources seen give nothing for 1969-2011. Still an open-air market. No coordinates found; the two sources disagree on dates.

name: Faculty of Medicine, University of Tripoli
text: Tripoli's medical school, opened in 1973 and located next to the university's main campus. Libya's medical schools opened in Benghazi (1970) and Tripoli (1973) on a British-style curriculum. The faculty has its own administration although it was planned as part of the main university, and trains students at Tripoli Medical Center, Tripoli Central Hospital, Al-Khadra and Al-Jalaa hospitals. Still an active faculty of the University of Tripoli. No coordinates were found for the faculty building itself.

name: Police headquarters, Tripoli (reported guard post)
text: A Tripoli police headquarters named in a 1982 press report as one of the places where Gaddafi posted his Syrian bodyguards. A report carried in JPRS Near East/North Africa Report No. 2475 (26 January 1982) quotes a newspaper saying Colonel Kadhafi had posted most of his 500-strong Syrian bodyguard around his palace, 'others are at the radio station and police headquarters.' The report does not say where the police headquarters stood. Single press report, location not given, and it is not shown to be the Military Police Command or the police college.

name: Libyan Open University
text: A distance-learning university based in Tripoli, established in 1987. History: Established in 1987 as an education foundation affiliated with the Ministry of Higher Education, it began scientific activity in the 1989/1990 academic year. Its mission was to spread distance learning without limits of place, time or age. It lists itself as a member of the Arab Universities Union and the Arab Network for Open Education Learning. No street address or coordinates found; only a Tripoli P.O. box was listed. Naser University and Libyan International Medical University could not be sourced (the latter is generally a Benghazi institution).

name: Tripoli Congress Center
text: A conference building of about 25,000 square metres designed by TA Tabanlioglu Architects and listed as built in 2009-2010. The architects list the client as the State of Libya, with a two-storey rectangular block wrapped in a metal mesh shield and set among woodland. Its listed date is 2009-2010. The sources seen do not state how it was used before 2011. Its present use is not described in the sources seen. No coordinates found. It is not confirmed whether this is the building owners call the Palace of Conferences or Dhafra Convention Centre.

name: Ahmed Pasha Karamanli Mosque
text: An 18th-century mosque complex in Tripoli's old city founded by Ahmed Karamanli, with a madrasa and tombs of the dynasty. History: Construction began in 1736 (inscriptions suggest 1737-38). No Gaddafi-era events were found. It was vandalised in 2014 during the civil war: ceramic tiles and marble decoration were damaged, and UNESCO condemned the attack. It is listed as active. No coordinates found.

name: Royal Miramare Theatre (demolished)
text: An Italian-era theatre across from the Red Castle, demolished under Gaddafi's government to create space for mass demonstrations. Built in 1928, it stood opposite the Red Castle on Martyrs' (then Green) Square. Gaddafi's government demolished it after the 1960s to make room for large demonstrations in the square. The theatre no longer exists. Exact demolition date and exact site are not given; no coordinates.

name: Darghouth Turkish Bath (Hammam Darghut)
text: A Turkish bath in the Old City founded around 1670 and attached to the Sidi Darghut mosque and tomb. The bath was established in 1081 AH (about 1670-1671), annexed to the Sidi Darghut mosque and tomb. The sources seen give no information on its use during the Gaddafi period. Its present state is not described in the sources seen. No coordinates found; present use and Gaddafi-era history are undocumented in the sources seen.

name: Ministry of Justice (Martyrs' Square)
text: A justice ministry building at Martyrs' Square that was burned in the February 2011 protests. The People's Hall article says demonstrators set fire to several buildings in February 2011, including the justice ministry at Martyrs' Square. The sources seen give no earlier history. Not described in the sources seen. The OSM extract shows a separate 'Ministry of Justice' point elsewhere in Tripoli, so exact building is unconfirmed; no coordinates given.

name: National Oil Corporation headquarters
text: The headquarters of Libya's National Oil Corporation in central Tripoli. The sources seen give no history before 2011. On 10 September 2018 armed men stormed the building, a blast followed, and a fire spread on lower floors; at least two staff and two gunmen died and ten were wounded. No coordinates found; Gaddafi-era use is not documented in the sources seen.

name: GMR Stadium (Al-Madina SC ground)
text: An 8,000-capacity football ground in Tripoli, home of Al-Madina SC. History: A timeline of Tripoli dates its opening to 2000. Al-Madina SC was founded on 29 October 1953 and is the only Libyan club never relegated. Al-Madina plays in the Libyan Premier League western group in 2025-26. No coordinates found. No sources were found for an Al-Ahli Tripoli club ground other than the national stadium, or for an indoor basketball arena.

name: Tripoli Central Railway Station (demolished)
text: The Italian-built central railway station of Tripoli, which was demolished under Gaddafi. Built under Italian rule, the station was demolished under Gaddafi, according to Wikipedia's article on Tripoli. The sources seen give no date or location. No station remains. Date of demolition and site are not given in the sources seen.

name: Uthman Pasha Madrasa
text: An Ottoman madrasa built in 1654 and one of the best-preserved in Tripoli, with a courtyard, student rooms and a domed tomb chamber. Wikipedia's article on Tripoli says it was built in 1654. The sources seen give no events for 1969-2011. Not described. No coordinates, no recent history.

name: Tripoli Fish Market
text: A busy seafood market at the edge of the Old City. The sources seen do not cover its history. A travel site describes a busy market selling sardines, mackerel, sea bream, shrimp and other seafood, with a cleaning area. No coordinates, history or 2011 information found.

name: Libyan Studies Centre
text: A research and historical documentation centre in Tripoli that opened in 1978. History: A timeline of Tripoli records that the Libyan Studies Center opened in 1978. Only the opening date was found; the Arabic name and the location are not confirmed here. The National Library was not found in the sources.

why: 77 detainees linked to the 1996 Abu Salim killings were held at al-Hadba on 17 May 2017 and later confirmed at Ain Zara in November 2017.
Former detainees describe interrogation elsewhere, then transfer to Jdeida, and being held in both Jdeida and Abu Salim.
Maktab al-Nasser held prisoners, many of whom were later moved on to Abu Salim; dates unverified.
After the 8 May 1984 attack on Bab al-Aziziya, most of those arrested were believed held at Abu Salim, whose first prisoners arrived in 1984.
The Internal Security Agency held full control of both Ain Zara and Abu Salim prisons, including detainees kept past their sentences.
Seventy-seven detainees tied to the 1996 Abu Salim killings were being held at al-Hadba in 2017 before their move to Ain Zara.
The 77 detainees linked to the 1996 Abu Salim killings were confirmed at Ain Zara in November 2017.
The June 1996 massacre happened inside Abu Salim prison, where about 1,200 prisoners were reportedly killed.
After the February 2011 protests, HRW feared Tripoli detainees were being held at Jdeida, Ain Zara and Abu Salim prisons.
HRW feared protesters seized after the 20 February 2011 shootings were held at Ain Zara among other prisons.
HRW heard that at least 50 bodies lay in the Abu Salim hospital morgue after the 21-22 February 2011 shootings; HRW also feared detainees were held at Abu Salim prison.
Amnesty placed al-Jdayda prison at al-Farnaj outside Tripoli, holding 24 students sentenced in 1995.
Jdeida prison was run by the General People's Committee of Justice, the Jamahiriya-era justice authority, when Amnesty visited in May 2009.
The curated Abu Salim site and the area profile describe the same prison, completed in 1984.
Both entries are the Ain Zara prison OpenStreetMap labels "the political prison".
In 2017 Abu Salim prison was held by the Central Security/Abu Salim armed group, per the UN.
On 2 May 2021 Libya's Supreme Court ruled the 1996 Abu Salim massacre a genocide and sent the case back to a lower court.
Senior Gaddafi-era figures including Saadi Gaddafi were held at al-Hadba prison during the post-2011 trial of the 2011 crackdown officials.
